# PLUGIN_REGISTERED Entry Point Notes

This page originally described `TilesRendererBase.js` as "the code entry point for PLUGIN_REGISTERED." The title is retained because old links and several code-reading notes point here; it is a convenient way to get readers close to the renderer's tile base class. The title itself should no longer be read as meaning that the registration implementation has been fully located.

The early margin note below has been retained: at the time, the file's location under `src/core/renderer/tiles/` led to the guess that plugin registration would sit at the same level as tile traversal. That guess narrowed the search too much. The filename and directory establish only that it belongs to the tiles renderer; they are no substitute for checking declarations, branches, and call sites section by section. The old notes are still useful because further reading can indeed start from the local entry point they identify; they are no longer a suitable basis for deciding where to make changes.

## The Four Edges in the File Header

The imports directly visible on review are still these lines:

```js
import { getUrlExtension } from '../utilities/urlExtension.js';
import { LRUCache } from '../utilities/LRUCache.js';
import { PriorityQueue } from '../utilities/PriorityQueue.js';
import { runTraversal } from './traverseFunctions.js';
```

These are not a set of parallel "plugin dependencies." `runTraversal` and the current directory are both on the tiles side, making that a useful place to start tracing how traversal gets back to the renderer object; the other three come in through `utilities`, and their names point to the URL suffix, a least-recently-used cache, and a priority queue, respectively. Someone previously equated `PriorityQueue` directly with the registration queue for PLUGIN_REGISTERED. No corresponding code supporting that inference was recorded on this page, so it is now marked as an old claim. Whether the queue participates in downloading or processing, and whether it is on the same path as the registration flag, needs to be determined from the actual reference sites.

When reading this file, first look at the imports separately from the members and constructor initialization that follow. The dependencies at the top of the file answer only "which local utilities this module can access," not at what lifecycle stage those utilities are called. When you encounter `runTraversal`, first note the objects and callbacks passed in nearby; if you see a cache or queue, also note whether the renderer holds the instance itself or it is passed in from outside. This makes it easier to keep track of object relationships than searching the entire repository for `PLUGIN_REGISTERED` and picking one hit.

The original draft put `getUrlExtension` in the "possibly unrelated" column. That conclusion was not solid either: at a minimum, it shows that this renderer file has access to URL processing utilities. This page does not go into whether that processing applies to overlays, tile content, or other resources. It is left without a functional label here, simply as a branch to follow while reading. Conversely, the presence of `LRUCache` alone does not establish the type of objects being cached; its initialization and read/write sites need to be checked within this file.

You can use this short review sequence to avoid mistaking names for behavior:

```text
TilesRendererBase.js
  ├─ runTraversal: first find local calls and the objects passed in
  ├─ PriorityQueue: then inspect members near creation, enqueueing, or cancellation
  ├─ LRUCache: check where cached values enter and where they are evicted
  └─ getUrlExtension: finally return to the reference sites to confirm the resource path
```

This diagram is only a code-reading order for this file; it does not mean the four edges necessarily run in sequence. The old version's idea of drawing them as a registration chain should no longer be used. In particular, a priority queue and a cache may appear in adjacent code while serving different stages of resource handling; only a member access or argument passing at the same site can connect them.

This update did not turn up a PLUGIN_REGISTERED declaration snippet that could be included directly on this page, so "entry point" is not being upgraded to "registration location." What can be confirmed at this point is that this JS module is a suitable starting point for inspecting the tiles renderer's local dependencies. The file header already provides four branches to explore: URL, caching, queues, and traversal. To continue, first document where `runTraversal` is actually used within this file, then decide whether to trace back through `PriorityQueue`. DOC-03 documents another example entry point and should not be used to fill in the call snippets missing here.

# Notes on tracing the _worldToTiles event

This old note has long been used to find `src/babylonjs/renderer/tiles/TilesRenderer.js`. The earliest reading tied `_worldToTiles` closely to `TransformNode`: on seeing a Babylon node type, it treated that type as the event output itself. That approach can get readers into the file, but makes it easy to stop at the first type name.

A later review of the file header kept the original pointer but crossed out that equivalence. `TransformNode` is just an object explicitly imported by this file; the same section also includes the renderer base class, loading utilities, math objects, and the frustum. Together, they make up the surrounding context visible when reading the file; they do not imply that `_worldToTiles` passes through each of these objects in turn. The original margin note remains:

> Start by treating `_worldToTiles` as a node output.

This works as a starting point for the first search, not as a basis for determining what form the output takes.

Four imports are directly visible in the file header:

```js
import { TilesRendererBase, LoaderUtils } from '3d-tiles-renderer/core';
import { TransformNode } from '@babylonjs/core/Meshes/transformNode';
import { Matrix, Vector3 } from '@babylonjs/core/Maths/math.vector';
import { Frustum } from '@babylonjs/core/Maths/math.frustum';
```

When reading this section, start by using `TilesRendererBase` as an entry point for tracing inheritance, rather than drawing a direct call path between it and `_worldToTiles`. `LoaderUtils` appears in the same import statement, which means it comes from the same core package as the base class; whether it is involved in that output needs to be checked in the context where the variable appears. `Matrix`, `Vector3`, and `Frustum` offer three concrete search directions: transforms, coordinate values, and the frustum. They are better than the broad label "event output" for narrowing down what to read within the file.

When tracing this in practice, you can work outward in both directions from occurrences of the name rather than read the whole file from top to bottom. First find the first assignment to `_worldToTiles` and note whether its right-hand expression contains a node, matrix, or vector; then find every read. If a read is immediately next to `Frustum`, classify that section as part of the visibility-related reading path; if it is next to `Matrix` or `Vector3`, initially classify it as part of the transform path. This "classification" is only a way to mark sections as you page through; it cannot replace assessing the adjacent statements.

```text
TilesRenderer.js
  ├─ TilesRendererBase / LoaderUtils
  ├─ TransformNode
  ├─ Matrix / Vector3
  └─ Frustum
       ↑
  Revisit these names starting from the _worldToTiles read/write sites
```

The old version recommended searching the entire file for `TransformNode` first, then going back to look for `_worldToTiles`. That order can still help you quickly get familiar with the object names on the Babylon side, but it is no longer the preferred approach. The sections around occurrences of the variable name are usually shorter, and make it easier to see what sits between a write and the next read. Especially when `Matrix` and `Vector3` appear together, first mark the value's source, transformation, and consumption sites separately; do not put every coordinate object at the same level just because the name contains world.

The old note also described `Frustum` as "the output's visibility switch." After review, only the narrower description was retained: it is a direct dependency in the file header, and is worth using as a search term around `_worldToTiles`. The old record left no snippets to check whether it serves as a condition, when it is read, or its order relative to the event output. The "switch" wording is kept here to explain why the early reading leaned toward the visibility path.

Another common detour is `LoaderUtils`. The name can easily lead readers toward resource loading, but its relationship to `_worldToTiles` was not recorded on this page. When you encounter this import, stop at its actual occurrences first: if those occurrences are not in statements adjacent to the variable, there is no need to trace the loading path just to fill in the story. The local goal for this file remains to reconstruct the sections where `_worldToTiles` is written and read on the Babylon side.

DOC-06 documents the rule entry point for CesiumIonAuthPlugi, a different search area from the variable output here; if both locations need to be checked, you can start with the object names on that page. This page retains only the `TilesRenderer.js` file header, the old node interpretation, and the reading order as revised later.

The old search notes put `wordWrap` and `utils/docs/RenderDocsUtils.js` on the same line. This label continued to be used, mainly because, when tracking down line-break issues in old documentation, the filename made it easier than the page name to get back to the same small section of code. - Only then return to the places that reference `RenderDocsUtils.js` and check whether the content passed in by the outer code has already undergone other processing.

The first draft treated "code entry point" as "place to make a change." That interpretation was later crossed out, but the original note is still worth keeping, because the only detail left in old issue descriptions is often that the text did not wrap as expected. Searching the whole repository from a results page, style name, or content field quickly turns up many pieces of processing code with the same name; starting at the `RenderDocsUtils.js` hit at least lets you first separate processing inside the file from display outside it.

A caller Fang Ke may already have processed the text before passing it in, and the outer code may continue processing after receiving the result. Likewise, the filename `RenderDocsUtils.js` cannot be used to infer all document display behavior. The first draft did not preserve any specific caller name, and the review did not invent one.

During review, the easiest point to miss is the "first exit from the file." If you stop at the line containing the `wordWrap` hit, you usually see only the local intent; if you immediately follow the name farther afield, it is easy to mix up several similar text-processing operations. When overlay updates are slow, the symptoms on screen get mixed together: some layers have already started hiding, while image processing still appears to be waiting; some layers appear late, and it is difficult to tell from the display alone whether downloading, processing, or the visibility transition is holding up the result. # Image Queue and Visibility Decision Record

The initial observation on the overlay path was vague: when updates were slow, a layer would sometimes no longer be displayed, while an image being processed was still described as waiting. The first draft separated downloading, processing, and visibility to avoid treating a single delay label as the sole cause. The second review kept that separation, added objects that could be confirmed from the file, and retained a working assumption that later proved too broad.

## Boundaries established in the first draft

A transition from visible to hidden only tells us that the layer's presentation state has changed. It does not tell us whether the image data has been obtained, whether it has entered processing, or whether the queue has removed the corresponding work item. Conversely, removing a work item is not sufficient evidence that the on-screen visibility transition has completed.

There were still two possibilities at that point:

1. The queue is owned by each overlay instance and stops along with the instance when it disappears;
2. The queue serves multiple instances; instance visibility only affects whether results continue to be used, not the capacity of the processing resources themselves.

The first draft did not choose a capacity value or define reordering rules after cancellation. The only decision was to continue examining `ImageOverlayPlugin.js`, leaving animation completion outside the queue conclusions.

## File structure observed during the review

The review focused on `src/three/plugins/images/ImageOverlayPlugin.js`. The file header showed:

```js
import { Color, BufferAttribute, Matrix4, Vector3, Box3, Triangle, CanvasTexture } from 'three';
import { PriorityQueue, PriorityQueueItemRemovedError } from '3d-tiles-renderer/core';
import { CesiumIonAuth, GoogleCloudAuth } from '3d-tiles-renderer/core/plugins';
import { XYZImageSource } from './sources/XYZImageSource.js';
```

These dependencies bring several easily conflated objects together in one place: geometry and texture objects used for rendering, the core queue and removal error, the authentication plugin, and the overlay image source. The review did not connect them into a complete execution chain; the questions at that point were only who owned the queue and where visibility changes were finalized.

The top of the file also contained:

```js
const _matrix = /* @__PURE__ */ new Matrix4();
const _vec = /* @__PURE__ */ new Vector3();
const _center = /* @__PURE__ */ new Vector3();
const _sphereCenter = /* @__PURE__ */ new Vector3();
```

Next, `_normal`, `_box`, and `SPLIT_TILE_DATA` were visible. The added note from this review is that these module-level objects support nearby calculations in the plugin file and should not be used as substitute evidence for the processing queue's scope. Someone had earlier summarized "top-level reuse in the file" as "all resources in the plugin reset per instance." That was too broad; it is retained below as the old position.

## Retained old position

> **Old record, no longer applicable:** If an overlay is hidden, its associated image processing should stop along with it; capacity can therefore initially be estimated based on visible instances.

That statement was intended to give the investigation at the time a direction. It treated visibility as a resource boundary and conflated "stopping" with three different things: cancellation, removal, and animation completion. After the review, it was no longer used as a basis for assessing the implementation, but it was not deleted: it explains why early checks prioritized the hide branch instead of checking the processing queue first.

## What this review did not resolve

The review only confirmed that `PriorityQueue` and `PriorityQueueItemRemovedError` were both imported via this plugin path. The former makes "queued processing work" a reasonable target for investigation; the latter indicates that removal has a path requiring separate handling. Together, they do not directly establish whether a particular instance owns the queue, whether a hide action necessarily removes work items, whether removal means resources have already been released, or whether visibility transitions are completed by the same callback.

The decision from this review is to retain "shared resource" as the stronger candidate and stop using the number of visible instances as a proxy for processing capacity. Animation completion will continue to be tracked as a state issue and must not be used as a basis for adjusting processing limits.

The review note left just one line: first distinguish "who picks up work" from "who ends the display." Follow-up checks should separately identify the entry point where work items start processing, the conditions under which work items are removed, and the state written back when a delayed show or hide completes. `XYZImageSource`, `CesiumIonAuth`, and `GoogleCloudAuth` are only nearby reading references in the same file, not a basis here for drawing conclusions about image sources or authentication policies.

# Image Queue and Visibility Decision Record

This record initially addressed only one narrow question: when overlay updates are slow, why do image-processing waits and visibility transitions appear in the same observed sequence. It was later used to trace back the capacity of the shared image-processing queue and to investigate when delayed showing and delayed hiding should be considered complete. The two threads have remained side by side because they were once mistakenly collapsed into the same problem.

The associated local entry is still `src/three/plugins/images/ImageOverlayPlugin.js`. The file itself is not an overview of the overlay system, but it has remained the readable reference point for this page's history: overlay image sources, the core queue type, queue-removal errors, and rendering-side temporary objects all appear here. Later addenda filled in decisions around only two points: who shares the processing work, and which completion signal visibility actions should not reuse.

## 2023-04-19: Initially splitting apart slow updates

The earliest record broke the situation down into "the work is still being processed" and "the layer is still transitioning." At the time, debugging relied heavily on screen state: if the layer was hidden, the associated work was assumed to stop; if the layer appeared late, the queue was assumed to have stopped consuming work. Both inferences treated what the user saw as the queue state.

The initial draft did not commit to a specific implementation; it only outlined two options. One option was for each overlay instance to have its own processing budget, so hiding an instance could stop that budget as well. The other was for overlay instances to use the same processing resource; an instance's visibility would affect only when the result became visible or whether the result was still worth submitting. The draft decided to read the code along the latter path for the time being, because "hide" and "remove" are not the same verb.

The short margin note left at the time was:

> Don't use display state to calculate capacity yet. First find where work items are removed; let the animation finish on its own.

This was not a complete interface contract. It merely prevented the initial investigation from writing down two unverified equivalences: hidden equals canceled, and canceled equals processing complete. Later reviews did not merge these three concepts back together either.

The earliest version also noted module-level temporaries near the front of the file: `_matrix`, `_vec`, `_center`, `_sphereCenter`, `_normal`, `_box` and `SPLIT_TILE_DATA`. At the time, someone collectively called the "top-level reusable objects" shared resources and further speculated that the queue would reset in a similar way. This analogy was not adopted. Temporary matrices, vectors, and bounding objects are working objects for local calculations; they are adjacent to the question of queue ownership, but are not the same thing.

The initial record did not write download queuing, image processing, and transitions as one chain. This was not because the three were unrelated, but because there was not enough evidence at the time to determine the order in which they completed. In particular, once hiding began, whether previously acquired image work continued running could not be read directly from the screen.

## Addendum left by the early review

The initial review did not call for immediately changing all visibility logic. Instead, it called for changing the order of evaluation: first ask what work the queue accepts, then ask when an instance stops accepting results, and only then ask when the transition ends. This order matters because an overlay being invisible on screen is not enough to establish that the processing it previously triggered has left the queue.

The review notes contained two reminders that had not been formalized into rules:

- The presence of `PriorityQueue` should direct attention to how work items are acquired, ordered, and removed, rather than just the layer's visibility state;
- `PriorityQueueItemRemovedError` must be read separately from normal completion. It points to an exception path related to removal and cannot inherently serve as a notification that the hide animation has ended.

Later, these two reminders were often merged into a single statement: "The queue will take care of everything." That was an overgeneralization. A queue can describe the capacity for processing work and the state of work items, but show/hide animations still need their own completion conditions. Having both concepts in the same file does not automatically establish the order in which they complete.

The initial review also deliberately left authentication objects out of the evaluation. `CesiumIonAuth`, `GoogleCloudAuth`, and `XYZImageSource` are all direct dependencies of the same file; they help readers confirm that this is an overlay-related path, but provide no conclusions about shared capacity or the completion of visibility changes. Authentication and image sources were kept on this page only to prevent later readers from treating all imports as queue configuration.

## 2023-10-10: File Review and Interim Decision

The second review returned to the same file. The following was visible at the top of the file:

```js
import { Color, BufferAttribute, Matrix4, Vector3, Box3, Triangle, CanvasTexture } from 'three';
import { PriorityQueue, PriorityQueueItemRemovedError } from '3d-tiles-renderer/core';
import { CesiumIonAuth, GoogleCloudAuth } from '3d-tiles-renderer/core/plugins';
import { XYZImageSource } from './sources/XYZImageSource.js';
```

This import block was retained not to explain each symbol individually. At the time, it answered a narrower question: the queue type and removal error come from the core package, while the overlay path also directly accesses local image sources. Readers should not infer from this that "image sources exist" means "each image source has its own processing queue," nor should they mistake temporary rendering objects for capacity counters.

During the same review, the four declarations near the beginning were copied out separately:

```js
const _matrix = /* @__PURE__ */ new Matrix4();
const _vec = /* @__PURE__ */ new Vector3();
const _center = /* @__PURE__ */ new Vector3();
const _sphereCenter = /* @__PURE__ */ new Vector3();
```

`_normal`, `_box`, and `SPLIT_TILE_DATA` are also nearby. This addendum treated them only as a dividing line when reading the code: on one side are reusable temporaries for geometric calculations, and on the other are queue objects in the overlay processing path. The review did not infer the work item lifecycle from these declarations, nor did it carry their names over into the evaluation of show/hide animations.

The interim decision reached after the review was to stop using "the number of currently visible instances" to estimate the actual capacity for image processing. On-screen visibility affects whether the caller still needs a particular result, but visibility itself cannot indicate that a work item has already left the processing sequence. This decision was narrower in scope than the initial direction; it did not cover every cancellation scenario, nor did it draw conclusions about download scheduling.

The queue creation point and the instance handoff point were still unconfirmed at the time. To avoid presenting a candidate explanation as an established fact, the record retained only the stronger lead of "shared resources", did not assign a numeric value to the capacity, and did not specify details such as whether reordering occurs after cancellation or whether result objects are released immediately after removal.

## Old Approach Retained in Place

The passage below was once used as a quick-fix recommendation, and its original meaning is preserved here, but it must no longer be treated as the current practice.

> **Deprecated handling recommendation:** Once an overlay enters the hiding transition, treat the instance's processing quota as having been returned; if the animation has not yet finished, prioritize waiting for the animation without needing to inspect the processing work item.

This recommendation seemed convenient at the time because it collapsed the hiding effect seen by users and the resource assessment into a single condition. The problem was that it did not distinguish among three states: the layer is being hidden, the queue work item has been removed, and image processing has finished. Subsequent review overturned it, not because the hiding action was meaningless, but because hiding can only factor into decisions about committing results and transitions, and cannot by itself prove that the quota has been returned.

The old recommendation was not removed from the document because it explains why the early investigation prioritized looking for animation callbacks rather than examining the queue first. If only today's conclusion were retained, later readers would not understand why this line of investigation ever existed and could easily once again document "animation completion" as the only resource-side signal.

Another abandoned simplification was "each plugin instance starts its own processing queue". It was only a candidate early on and was never proven. It did make local observations easy to explain: when an overlay disappeared, it seemed to affect only its own work; but this explanation could not account for whether different instances competed for the same quota, or where the capacity should be set. Subsequent work did not pursue ad hoc fixes along these lines, but instead reframed the problem as verifying the sharing relationship.

## A Field Record with No Established Cause

One field record documented "the layer is no longer displayed" alongside "the image being processed is still described as waiting". It did not preserve enough information to attribute the wait to downloading, priority sorting, or image processing; therefore, it should not be retroactively rewritten as any particular type of failure. Its only value is as a counterexample: the display state and processing state can change at the same time without necessarily sharing the same completion condition.

This field record also exposed the shortcomings of the earlier investigation. When the quota was estimated from the number of visible overlays, instances in the process of hiding, work that was already queued but had not yet affected the display, and the question of whether multiple instances were contending for resources were all left out of the observations. As a result, different people's estimates would not match, yet there was no way to identify whether the discrepancy arose in the display layer or the processing layer.

To facilitate further discussion, the work item states are shown in the diagram below. It only distinguishes processing work from the removal path and does not interpret any edge as a state change in the show/hide animation.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    state "Queued work" as queued
    state "Processing" as processing
    state "Removed" as removed
    state "Completed" as completed
    [*] --> queued
    queued --> processing
    processing --> removed
    processing --> completed
    removed --> [*]
    completed --> [*]
```

"Completed" in the diagram only means that the processing work is no longer in the processing state; it is not synonymous with "the layer is already visible" or "the layer is already hidden." "Removed" likewise only preserves a distinction for reading the queue and must not be changed into an alias for the end of the animation.

## Separate closure for delayed visibility

The records for delayed show/hide animations must be independent of downloading and processing. For a show delay, the caller cares about when the layer is allowed to enter the visible state; for a hide delay, the caller cares about when it should no longer treat the layer as being displayed. Both may coexist with image processing in the same update loop, but this does not require them to use the same end condition.

Here, "closure" means that the show/hide state is no longer left pending, not that all related resources have generally finished cleanup. This distinction was added later: if the end of a transition is directly treated as the queue being empty, the result of slow processing will be misinterpreted; if removal of a work item is directly treated as the end of the animation, the screen state will in turn be misinterpreted.

Therefore, each side needs an explicit, readable check:

- The processing side focuses on whether the work item is still in the queue, whether it has been removed, and whether the result is still allowed to enter the subsequent path;
- The show/hide side focuses on whether the show or hide transition has completed, and, after completion, no longer maintains an intermediate state;
- When the two sides meet, the decision is whether the result can be adopted, not renaming one side's completion signal and handing it to the other side.

This does not introduce an additional state machine. It only separates terms that were mixed together in the earlier records. A previously started processing operation may still exist after the overlay is hidden; after the processing work is removed, the show/hide transition may still be in its own state. Every on-site check should first state which side is being observed.

## 2025-09-04: Entry point for capacity review

The capacity issue later received a dedicated maintenance entry. GEO-201 records the current version's request to verify the capacity of the shared image-processing queue and follows the retrieval wording of `maxJobs = 10`. This entry is only responsible for bringing the verification back to the relevant maintenance object; this page retains the decision process explaining why capacity cannot be inferred from a single instance or an animation state.

This review did not change the earlier boundaries for showing and hiding. It only requires that the "number of visible instances" no longer be used as a substitute for processing capacity, and that an instance entering a hide transition not be interpreted as having already released its exclusive resources. Capacity is assessed at queue scope; showing and hiding are assessed within the visibility path.

During the meeting, the issues were divided into two columns. One was "shared capacity", which examined who provides the work quota, whether instances compete with one another, and how removed work is handled. The other was "delayed showing and hiding", which examined the actions after which showing and hiding respectively stop waiting. Only one connection was drawn between the two columns: before a result is committed, confirm that the layer can still accept it.

This meeting side note did not produce a new implementation plan, but it prevented a common change: directly reducing the processing queue's work quota to make hiding faster. That would shift the pressure of the visual transition onto processing scheduling, without explaining either why processing should stop or how a lower quota would improve hide completion. The decision after the meeting was to review capacity adjustments and animation completion separately; any change that ties the two together should first explain the connection point.

## Current decision, 2025-09-05

Following the records and review above, this page makes an explicit decision on capacity: All ImageOverlayPlugin instances use one shared process queue, and that queue has maxJobs = 10.

This statement addresses only the scope and capacity of the image-processing queue. It does not recast download scheduling as the same thing, nor does it define the lifecycles of authentication plugins, image sources, or rendering objects. `ImageOverlayPlugin.js` remains the starting point for reference: start here when you need to understand the types and temporary objects around overlay processing; when you need to determine whether an anomaly concerns showing, hiding, removal, or capacity contention, first classify the observed signals on the appropriate side.

The resulting decision on showing and hiding is equally narrow in scope: completion of delayed showing and delayed hiding should be handled within the visibility path, and cannot be replaced by checking whether the shared processing queue still has work. The shared queue limits the concurrency with which all instances collectively can enter processing; it is not an animation timer, nor is it another name for "the layer has disappeared from view".

With capacity fixed, the earlier practice of "estimating quotas per instance" no longer applies. When examining an overlay, do not assume that its exclusive quota has been released simply because it is hidden—the current decision does not allocate exclusive quotas to instances. What must be checked separately is whether the instance might still receive processing results, and whether the corresponding work item is still in the processing path. These are visibility and queue assessments, respectively.

## Adjacent issue, not yet split into a separate page

One closely related issue remains undecided here: once the hide transition begins, where to determine whether image-processing results that have already been obtained but are not yet complete can still be used. This is not a counterexample to "whether the queue is shared", but a question of commit conditions where the shared queue meets the visibility path.

Existing records are sufficient to require that this judgment not be hidden in a capacity constant, and that we not assume at the point where the animation completes that all processing has stopped. If anything is added later, it should only cover the handoff between result submission and visibility-state changes; this page should not be expanded into a general explanation of downloads, authentication, and rendering objects.

Another adjacent issue is the processing semantics of `PriorityQueueItemRemovedError`. Existing records only confirm that it is part of the core queue import and that it should be read separately from normal completion; this page does not define a strategy for retrying it, ignoring exceptions, or converting it into an animation state. This gap needs to be preserved, to prevent readers from mistaking "removal errors have been mentioned" for an existing handling rule.

## Legacy Examples Appendix

### Legacy Example A: Estimating Capacity from the Number of Visible Overlay Images

Earlier, the number of overlay images still visible in the scene was used as an approximation of the processing capacity. This example was convenient for manual assessment, but omitted hidden instances, work that had already been queued but had not yet affected the display, and the possibility of resources being shared among instances. Once the current capacity was determined, this estimation method was no longer used; it is retained only to explain why the numbers in the old troubleshooting table do not match one another.

### Legacy Example B: Hidden Means Processing Complete

Another old note described the hide action as "clearing the processing for that layer." It should now be read as the working assumption at the time, not as the action definition. Hiding indicates that a state change along the visibility path has started or completed; processing completion, work-item removal, and whether the result has been submitted need to be confirmed separately. The old note is useful only for marking where the misjudgment occurred.

### Reading Markers Beside the Files

During review, first distinguish the following groups of names:

- `Matrix4`, `Vector3`, `Box3`, `Triangle`, and `CanvasTexture` belong to rendering and computation adjacency;
- `_matrix`, `_vec`, `_center`, `_sphereCenter`, `_normal`, `_box`, and `SPLIT_TILE_DATA` are local declarations visible within the file;
- `PriorityQueue` and `PriorityQueueItemRemovedError` point to processing work and its removal path;
- `XYZImageSource` points to the overlay image source.

This grouping is not an interface inventory, nor does it require these objects to change at the same pace. It merely helps people who later enter `ImageOverlayPlugin.js` avoid the old misread: do not see a module-level variable and assert that resources are exclusive to each instance, and do not see a layer being hidden and assert that shared processing has already ended.

# Empty-content tiles and character caching proposal

This review starts by documenting two points separately that could easily end up being changed together: the state left behind when empty-content tiles are released, and the cost of repeatedly retrieving character metrics for polyline labels. Don't tie character-metric caching to the tile-release change yet. We first need to find where metrics are actually retrieved after polyline projection, then decide whether the cache should be tied to labels, font materials, or a single tile update. # Proposal for empty-content tiles and character caching

This proposal originally put empty-content tile disposal and Polyline Character Metrics Cache in the same round of API review because both surface during visible tile updates. That decision to combine them did not hold up. The former is about whether a tile remains in traversal's view after disposal; the latter is about repeated metric reads during label rendering. Putting them in the same patch would only make it impossible to tell, during a rollback, whether the cost came from state cleanup or cache invalidation.

## First, drop the old visibility assumption

The v1 idea was to handle a tile with no content as a normal hide operation, then add the active-related actions. This description is kept here to explain why we connected the disposal branch to the visibility API at the time: the visible and active states coexisted, which made it look as though they should be cleared together.

Rechecking `src/core/renderer/tiles/TilesRendererBase.js` showed that the counterexample was precisely the combination of "still visible, still active, but no longer has renderable content". Here we need to clear the leftover traversal state, not add another round of visibility notifications for a renderable that does not exist. The old proposal's approach of "disposing through the normal path" is no longer being adopted; it would disguise the special empty-content branch as one where the object can still be displayed.

The API contract is now fixed: Disposing a visible, active tile with no renderable content clears its traversal state, calls setEmptyTileVisible(tile, false), and does not invoke renderable visibility or active hooks.

The point of this constraint is not to make all disposal uniform. Regular tiles are still handled according to their existing renderable relationships; this is limited to the empty-content branch. Both implementation and review should start with that branch, confirm that traversal state is cleared, and confirm that `setEmptyTileVisible(tile, false)` is where externally visible state is finalized. Do not add renderable visibility or active hooks just for "symmetry"; they have no object to operate on and would instead mask an incorrect lifecycle assumption.

## Character metrics will not land with the disposal branch

Polyline Character Metrics Cache remains a valid direction for performance work, but we do not yet have enough material to define it as an API shared with tile disposal. The existing entry points for reading the code show `LRUCache`, `PriorityQueue`, and `runTraversal` next to one another. This only helps locate the areas to examine next: whether the cache sits close to the labels themselves, whether it is affected by polyline screen projection, and whether sliced update triggers repeated reads. They do not automatically provide a cache key or invalidation conditions.

So this round retains only one narrowly scoped proposal: first identify where character metrics are read and what holds the return values, then assess whether there is a stable boundary for reuse. If the metrics are tied to glyph material, discussion of the cache design should center on material changes; if the reads occur in projected polyline segments, we first need to explain whether the old values can still be used when the segments change. These two cases cannot be combined under the same "cache per tile" description, because changes to a tile's visibility, content, and projection are not the same kind of change.

We previously considered directly reusing the existing `LRUCache`, but are not proceeding with that step. Without clear sources of invalidation, choosing a container will not solve incorrect reuse; hooking the character cache into `PriorityQueue` is not an alternative either. The queue handles work ordering; it does not say when metric results expire. The cache trial should be submitted separately to avoid changing the disposal sequence for empty-content tiles.

## Merge scope

Empty-content disposal can proceed to implementation review independently. The checks are whether the special-case tile stops participating in the old traversal state and whether it goes only through the designated empty-content visibility finalization point. If integration shows that renderable visibility or active hooks must be called to preserve existing behavior, back out that integration and recheck the callers rather than temporarily adding callbacks back in to pass local checks.

Character-metric caching remains in the investigation phase. Before implementation starts, at a minimum identify the read sites, what will be reused, and the invalidation triggers. If any one of these is still guesswork, do not include the cache in this release. This preserves separate rollback paths for the two issues: the disposal branch can be reverted independently, and the cache trial will not affect the tile's traversal state.

# Overlay Scheduling and Usage Troubleshooting Tree

When an overlay appears after the area has come into view, or the view looks like it has stopped changing but tile usage has not settled, first record these as two separate issues. There are only two starting points here: overlay download scheduling and tile usage flush.

The initial working assessment was: when an overlay is late, first check the order of events around the image request; when usage has not cleared, first wait for the view update to finish. This assessment was only for triage at the time; it does not mean the two paths share state, or that one can explain the other just because they occurred together once.

```text
Overlay appears late
├─ Was the address changed before the request was made
│  └─ Yes: record the transformed value, then revisit where it was processed
└─ No change to the address
   └─ Check whether any downloads are already waiting

Usage has not settled
├─ View is still changing
│  └─ Check again after this round of updates finishes
└─ View is stable
   └─ Record the tiles still considered in use
```

For the overlay side, start with `src/three/plugins/images/ImageOverlayPlugin.js`. # Overlay Scheduling and Occupancy Troubleshooting Tree

This page still uses two symptoms: the overlay does not appear in time, and tile occupancy does not clear in sync after the display settles. The previous version grouped both under "the current update has not finished." After review, that wording is too broad; retain it as an early field note, but no longer use it as a troubleshooting conclusion.

On the overlay side, don't start by asking whether the network has responded. First determine whether the image address has been processed, then check whether any download work is waiting. If the address has changed and no waiting item is visible, the issue is still before work submission; if a waiting item exists but the request status is unclear, don't write the wait up as a network failure. On the occupancy side, first ask whether the display is still changing. While it is still changing continuously, don't call the occupancy leftover; only when the display is stable and occupancy remains do we need to pin down the specific tile.

```text
Start: overlay or occupancy state is not as expected
│
├─ Overlay does not appear in time
│  │
│  ├─ Has the address been processed?
│  │  ├─ No or unclear: add the pre- and post-processing values
│  │  └─ Yes: continue
│  │
│  ├─ Is download work already waiting?
│  │  ├─ No: revisit the submission point in the image plugin
│  │  └─ Yes: retain the waiting state
│  │
│  └─ Has the request started?
│     ├─ Yes: exit the scheduling branch
│     └─ Unclear: record the address and waiting item; do not add a network conclusion
│
└─ Tile occupancy has not cleared
   │
   ├─ Is the display still updating?
   │  ├─ Yes: wait until the current update finishes, then check again
   │  └─ No: continue
   │
   ├─ Can you identify the tile that is still occupied?
   │  ├─ No: add the object first
   │  └─ Yes: retain the object and display state
   │
   └─ Does the occupancy disappear in a subsequent update?
      ├─ Yes: record it as delayed clearing
      └─ No: leave the object; continue checking around flush
```

`src/three/plugins/images/ImageOverlayPlugin.js` remains the first follow-up checkpoint for the overlay. The file header shows three's `Color`, `BufferAttribute`, `Matrix4`, `Vector3`, `Box3`, `Triangle`, and `CanvasTexture`, and also introduces core's `PriorityQueue` and `PriorityQueueItemRemovedError`. The image-source path also shows `XYZImageSource`. These objects indicate that the image plugin needs to handle geometry, source, and queued work at the same time; they do not show that all visible delays are caused by the queue.

The `_matrix`, `_vec`, `_center`, `_sphereCenter`, `_normal`, and `_box` at the start of the file are all work objects. Earlier, someone interpreted `_sphereCenter` as the source of overlay priority and `SPLIT_TILE_DATA` as flush data. The review found no records sufficient to support either interpretation. They are appropriate to retain as code-location names, but not to describe as causes of scheduling or occupancy.

## Deprecated Fast Path

The old approach was: when the overlay arrived late, assume that processing the address would directly issue the request; when occupancy had not cleared, assume that the same request had not finished. This fast path collapsed address processing, queuing, and the actual request into a single action, and tied the on-screen occupancy state to the image request. This wording still appears in old issue records, so leave it in place; do not use it for subsequent troubleshooting.

One review pass split the observations into three records: the values before and after address processing, whether a waiting item appeared, and whether the occupancy object disappeared in a subsequent frame. This did not produce a single cause, but it ruled out an easily confused case: a late overlay and delayed occupancy appearing in the same cycle does not mean the former caused the latter.

When the overlay branch reaches "the request has started," subsequent network or image-processing issues are no longer handled on this page. In the occupancy branch, if the display is stable but no specific tile can be identified, do not use "flush is out of sync" as the conclusion. flush remains a boundary for investigation here, not a confirmed fault location.

The image module also introduces `XYZImageSource`, but this page does not tie it to any particular delay. If the address processing and waiting item both line up but the overlay is still abnormal, continue tracing from the source object; don't instead make the source object the default place to assign responsibility for every overlay issue.

The tile-occupancy side still lacks stable samples. At this point, the only things to record are: whether the display is still changing, which tile is still considered occupied, and whether it later disappears on its own.

# Overlay Scheduling and Occupancy Troubleshooting Tree

This page has long been used to handle two seemingly similar situations: the visible area has changed, but the overlay has not appeared in the results in time; the view is no longer changing continuously, but a tile is still considered to be in use. They can easily occur in the same cycle, and for that reason they were once written up as a causal chain. The purpose of retaining the old paragraphs is not to prove that chain holds, but to let later investigations see where it once mixed observations with inferences.

The current procedure is still narrowly scoped. First choose a branch based on the symptom, and record the objects that branch requires; stop when you reach a stopping condition. Once the overlay request has started, networking and image processing are not explored further on this page. On the tile side, if no specific object has been identified, flush is not treated as the cause either. Both sides can be recorded at the same time, but do not start by writing down a shared root cause just because both seem slow in the same view.

| Symptom | What to record first | When to stop here |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The overlay does not appear in the visible results in time | The address before and after processing, whether a waiting entry appears | The request is confirmed to have started, or the object is not an image overlay |
| Occupancy remains after the view stabilizes | The specific tile, the state of the view, whether the occupancy disappears later | The tile cannot be identified, or the view is still updating continuously |

"Stop" in the table does not mean ignoring the problem. It simply separates scheduling, networking, image processing, and tile state to avoid inventing state where there is no observed object.

## 2023-03-20: The Initial Field Guidance

The earliest draft had only two entry points. When a visible overlay arrived late, check the request first; when occupancy did not clear, first wait for updates to finish. There was no complete reproduction of the scene at the time, so this passage was originally just an ad hoc triage guide, not a judgment about the implementation. Older records later interpreted "check the request first" too broadly, collapsing distinct points before and after the request into one.

The diagram from that time is still here. It can explain why the two symptoms appeared on the same page, but it cannot serve as the current procedure.

```text
Visible area changes
├─ Overlay does not appear → Check the request
└─ Occupancy does not clear → Wait for updates
```

The diagram does not say how far to follow the request, nor does it require recording which tile is still in use. The fact that "slow overlay" and "uncleared occupancy" appeared next to each other in early records only shows that they were observed during the same rendering interval, not that they shared a queue, a lock, or a callback.

That version also treated the queue type that appeared near the image plugin as a direct clue. Part of that judgment is still useful: reading for the overlay branch can start at `src/three/plugins/images/ImageOverlayPlugin.js`. Another part later proved to be an overreach: the presence of a queue object at the top of the file is not enough to show that all late arrivals are queue problems.

## Early Annotations Alongside the File

The top of the image plugin file shows `Color`, `BufferAttribute`, `Matrix4`, `Vector3`, `Box3`, `Triangle`, `CanvasTexture`. The same location also imports `PriorityQueue`, `PriorityQueueItemRemovedError`, and `XYZImageSource`. This set of imports led early investigators to group addresses, queued work, and image sources around a single starting point for reading the code.

The file also contains `_matrix`, `_vec`, `_center`, `_sphereCenter`, `_normal`, `_box` and `SPLIT_TILE_DATA`. These names were treated in the first round of notes as reference points that could be revisited. Two side notes later became misleading: one treated `_sphereCenter` as the central point for overlay priority; the other treated `SPLIT_TILE_DATA` as evidence that flush had already occurred. Neither recorded any supporting object states or call order.

Therefore, these names are now retained only as aids for reading the code. When you need to find geometry calculations, temporary vectors, or split data, you can start with them; do not place them in the overlay request sequence based on their names, or use them to identify the final handling point for tile occupancy.

## Early on-call side note: Wait one more cycle

During early on-call shifts, when occupancy persisted after the view had stabilized, a common response was to wait for another update. In some samples, it disappeared on its own after the wait, so "wait one more cycle" was briefly treated as a remedy. This action was not removed later, because it may still be necessary in the field to distinguish between a view that has not finished updating and one that is truly stable; however, it is no longer considered a recovery measure.

It left two questions unaddressed: which tile had been left behind before the wait, and whether the view changed again during the wait. Without the object and the before-and-after states, "it disappeared later" only means that the observation period was extended, not that flush had synchronized as expected. Every place in the old notes that only says "just wait a bit and it will be fine" lacks these two observations.

There was a similar side note on the overlay side: as soon as URL was seen to have been processed, the request was assumed to be on its way. This judgment was also incomplete. An address change only shows that processing occurred; it does not indicate whether the download job has been submitted, nor whether network activity has started. The early samples did not record both the original address and the processed address, making it impossible later to reconstruct the process from the single statement "URL was changed".

## 2023-06-22: The first review separated three states

The review did not produce a complete cross-module trace, but it split the overlay image records into three checkpoints: whether the address had been processed, whether there was pending download work, and whether the request had started. This breakdown was not intended to provide more explanation, but to avoid calling all three different points "fetch is complete".

Tile occupancy was also narrowed down to three observations: whether the display was still updating at the time of observation, which tile was still considered occupied, and whether that object disappeared during subsequent updates. If the first item still says "updating", do not call the behavior a cleanup failure; if the second item is empty, discussion of flush cannot continue; if the object in the third item has already disappeared, recording "delayed cleanup" is more accurate than "permanent retention".

The review tree at the time is shown below. It had more stopping points than the initial diagram, but still contained a gap that would need to be corrected later: the relationship between pending items and actual requests was not clearly documented.

```text
Overlay image does not appear in time
├─ Has the address changed
│  ├─ No or unclear → Record the values before and after processing
│  └─ Yes
├─ Is there pending download work
│  ├─ No → Return to the submission point
│  └─ Yes → Record the pending state
└─ Has the request started
   ├─ Yes → Leave the scheduling branch
   └─ Unclear → Do not record a network failure

Occupancy persists after the display stabilizes
├─ Is the display still updating
│  ├─ Yes → Wait for updates to finish
│  └─ No
├─ Can the tile be identified
│  ├─ No → Record the object first
│  └─ Yes
└─ Does it disappear during subsequent updates
   ├─ Yes → Delayed cleanup
   └─ No → Stay near flush
```

This separation ruled out a common but unsupported claim: because late overlay image arrival and prolonged occupancy occurred together, the image request must have held up the tile state. The review could confirm only two concurrent phenomena; it could not fill in the state handoff between them.

## Deprecated: Equating visual order with priority

An intermediate version tried calling all overlay images that arrived later "low priority". This approach was easy to read, because the image plugin introduced `PriorityQueue`, and there was indeed a visible order of arrival. But "arrived later" alone did not indicate whether the work had been submitted, whether it was pending, or whether its request had already started, nor did it indicate the work's priority in the queue.

Another combined line of reasoning was: the overlay image has not appeared, so the download has not finished; the download has not finished, so adjacent tiles will remain occupied; therefore, flush keeps being delayed. This reasoning was once used to explain two symptoms in the same round. Its problem was in the second step: no object records linked the image download to the occupancy of adjacent tiles. Imports at the top of the file, temporary vectors, and temporal proximity on screen could not replace that link.

This combined approach is now marked **no longer applicable**. It is retained because older issue descriptions may still use wording such as "the download is holding up flush". When encountering such a description, first return to the four types of observations: the address, pending items, request start, and the specific tile. Do not elevate the original wording into a current conclusion.

Also no longer used is the assumption that "if it disappears after waiting through one update, that means there is no problem." Disappearance after waiting supports only "it was not continuously retained at that time"; it cannot show that there was no earlier delay, nor prove that any image request was the cause. The old on-call step can still be used to distinguish whether the display is still changing, but it cannot be used as a shortcut for attribution.

## A comparison record that failed to converge

During review, we tried to put the two symptoms in the same view into a single comparison record: one side recorded address handling and the waiting item, while the other recorded the tile after the view stabilized. This attempt did not produce a common cause, but it exposed gaps in the old wording.

Some overlay samples can confirm only that the address was processed, not whether a waiting item appeared; some occupancy samples show only that the display looked static, without retaining the specific tile. Forcing these missing pieces together would only create false conclusions such as "queue blockage" or "flush was not triggered." The comparison record was therefore changed to two parallel tracks rather than one chain.

On the overlay track, when the address has changed but no waiting work has yet been seen, stop at the point where work is submitted inside the image plugin. When a waiting item is already present, waiting is the current observable fact; do not write it as success, failure, or cancellation. Once the request has started, continuing to trace the network or image processing falls under a different boundary.

On the tile track, while the display is still updating, do not label the problem as occupancy not yet being closed out. Only record the tile's subsequent state once the display is stable and the tile can be identified; if the object has not disappeared, leave a flush adjacency for further inspection. There is no evidence here to attribute any kind of lingering occupancy to the image queue.

## Language constraints left by the review

Subsequent review required "queue," "request," and "occupancy" to be used separately. The old draft often alternated among these three terms within the same paragraph, making it easy for readers to mistake a waiting item for network status and display occupancy for download status. The constraints adopted in the revision are as follows:

- When discussing the queue, write only whether the work has been submitted and whether it is still waiting;
- When discussing requests, write only whether the network request has started;
- When discussing occupancy, write only whether the specific tile is still considered occupied after the display stabilizes;
- When the object cannot be observed, write "unclear"; do not fill in the unknown as cancellation, failure, or residual state;
- When two phenomena appear at the same time, record them separately in their respective branches, then determine whether there is other material that can connect them.

The review also retained one unresolved edge case: when late overlays and lingering occupancy repeatedly appear in the same round, whether a common upstream condition exists. The current record has no object that can span both sides, so no "common root cause" node is added to the tree. This question remains open.

There is also one caveat regarding the geometric temporary objects from `_matrix` to `_box`. Visual position changes can easily lead people to associate geometric objects with scheduling order, but currently they are merely reference points for reading the image plugin. When geometric logic needs to be examined, you can continue from these declarations; do not treat them as explanations for overlay requests or flush behavior.

## 2024-11-25: Current branch

The currently usable tree states the stopping conditions more explicitly. It does not attempt to replace follow-up investigation of the network, image processing, or tile state; it only ensures that, before entering those branches, the field record does not record the state incorrectly.

```text
Symptom: The overlay did not make it into the visible result in time
│
├─ Can you confirm that the object is an image overlay?
│  ├─ No → Stop; do not apply the image plugin path
│  └─ Yes
│
├─ Has the address already been preprocessed?
│  ├─ Unclear → Record the values before and after processing, then return to address handling
│  └─ Yes
│
├─ Has a pending download job appeared?
│  ├─ No → Check where the job is submitted within the image plugin
│  └─ Yes
│
└─ Has the request already started?
   ├─ Yes → Stop; do not handle subsequent steps through the scheduling branch
   └─ Unclear → Keep only the pending state and the address

Symptom: Tiles are still considered occupied after the display stabilizes
│
├─ Is the display still updating?
│  ├─ Yes → Wait for the current update to finish, then return to this branch
│  └─ No
│
├─ Can you identify the tile that is still occupied?
│  ├─ No → Stop; identify the object first
│  └─ Yes
│
├─ Does the occupancy disappear during a subsequent update?
│  ├─ Yes → Record it as delayed closeout; do not classify it as a permanent residue
│  └─ No → Retain the object and display state, and continue investigating flush adjacency
│
└─ Is the overlay also late?
   ├─ Yes → Open a separate overlay branch; do not merge the attribution
   └─ No → Do not enter the image plugin
```

When the overlay branch reaches the job submission point, limit the inspection scope to the image-plugin adjacency around `src/three/plugins/images/ImageOverlayPlugin.js`. `PriorityQueue` and `PriorityQueueItemRemovedError` indicate that queuing and removal semantics should be distinguished; `XYZImageSource` is the entry point for the image-source path. They are all in the file header, but that does not allow cancellation, source selection, and tile occupancy to be written as one necessary chain.

Here we explicitly correct the old-version statement that "a request is sent directly after address processing." ImageOverlay.fetch submits a finite-priority job through downloadQueue.add and runs the network request from that queued callback against the URL it was given. It does not apply preprocessURL. CesiumIonOverlay.fetch and GoogleMapsOverlay.fetch apply preprocessURL before their own queued network request when that function is present.

This requirement only determines the order in overlay download scheduling. It does not answer whether the network request ultimately succeeds, nor does it stipulate when any tile occupancy must disappear. Once the request starts from the queued callback, stop at the scheduling branch; if occupancy remains after the display stabilizes, return to the specific tile and flush adjacency, and do not infer that the image request is still pending.

## Old cancellation-related branch

`PriorityQueueItemRemovedError` led the troubleshooter to add one unverified hypothesis: whenever the overlay image arrives late, assume that the work was removed and then added again. This hypothesis did not become a current rule. This category can only remind the investigator that queue removal is a case requiring distinction near the image block; when there is no actual object and no state change, it cannot be written as the explanation for this occurrence.

If the waiting item is no longer present during observation, first record "The waiting item is gone." Do not immediately call it cancellation, success, or failure. The three outcomes require different observations; this page provides no basis for substituting one for another. Earlier, directly writing "the image never arrived" as cancellation made it impossible to later recover what was actually observed at the time.

## Tile occupancy is still relatively narrow on one side

"Tile Occupancy flush Sync Closeout" remains a boundary to investigate on this page. The only actions supported by the existing records are: confirm the specific tile, determine whether the display is still updating, and then observe whether the occupancy disappears. They do not support writing the implementation location, trigger order, or responsible module of flush as a conclusion.

When the occupancy does indeed persist after the display stabilizes, the record should remain close to the observation: the tile identifier, whether an overlay image was late at the time, and whether any new display changes occurred afterward. The overlay image being late at the same time can only be treated as a co-occurring phenomenon; it should not be written as a trigger condition. If the occupancy later disappears, do not delete the original record; it indicates that closeout was delayed, not that the earlier observation did not exist.

## Old appendix: readable, but should not be followed

The following shorthand retains its original short-sentence form. The entire section is outdated:

```text
Overlay image late: first assume URL will make a request as soon as processing is complete;
Occupancy remains: first assume the request has not finished;
Both occur: check the queue first.
```

The first sentence omitted the boundary between submitting work and the queued callback; the second conflated the image request with the tile state; the third treated temporal co-occurrence as causation. They are no longer suitable as an operational path, but they can still explain why old records placed the image plugin and flush under the same heading.

Another old practice was to look for priority starting from `_sphereCenter`, then look for flush starting from `SPLIT_TILE_DATA`. It is retained in the appendix to remind readers that these variable names once led to an incorrect reading. The current branch does not follow this path; start with address handling, waiting work, request start, and the specific tile.

## Items not yet disentangled

If stable samples are obtained later, the most valuable additions would be the state in which the same tile was considered occupied before and after the display stabilized, as well as records of overlay address handling and the waiting item from the same round. Only then can we test whether the two branches merely occurred in parallel, rather than continuing to rely on speculation from the old page.

Until then, this page ends here: investigate the overlay image at three points—address handling, submission of waiting work, and request start; investigate the tile by display state, the specific object, and whether it subsequently disappears. The old combined attribution remains in the appendix and can no longer be treated as a conclusion.

# Overlay download cancellation experiment log

These notes originally split overlay download cancellation into two parts: the request stopping, and the download queue no longer retaining the pending item. The first two versions didn't clearly document the values passed between the two, making it easy during review to mistake "the queue eventually had one fewer item" for evidence that the cancellation branch was correct.

## Review excerpt

This round of review still starts at `src/three/plugins/images/ImageOverlayPlugin.js`. At the top of the file, you can find `_matrix`, `_vec`, `_center`, `_sphereCenter`, `_normal`, `_box`, and `SPLIT_TILE_DATA`.
