# Invisible Geometry Tile Lock Decision Record

This record was originally included in the Quality and Regression materials for MVT-R2026.09. The name carried over from the requirements discussions, but it has never denoted a single object that can be located directly by name: whether geometry tiles are visible, whether content is empty, whether batched meshes still retain resources, and whether the rendering side is still processing the relevant state are separate questions that need to be investigated individually.

The early version of the page described `src/three/plugins/batched/BatchedTilesPlugin.js` as "the entry point for the lock". This wording was retained later because the earlier investigation really did lead here from the issue name and call names; it helps whoever takes over open the same file first, but does not mean this has been proven to be where the lock is implemented. This distinction was not made clear at the time, leading some people to mistake the choice of entry point for a determination of ownership.

## The 2025 Assessment Retained

The original assessment was: do not yet create a separate runtime-mechanism explanation for this behavior, and continue to treat it as a quality regression item. This was not because all call relationships were already known, but because there was no material at the time to support equating "invisible" directly with "empty content", nor to support equating it with the download queue, processing queue, or cancellation of overlay downloads.

This assessment had two practical implications.

- During review, first examine resource and mesh connections near the batching plugin, rather than deriving function names from the requirement name.
- Any sample can only help reproduce a particular view or state, and cannot by itself define the boundaries between content locks, geometry locks, and queue retention.

More convenient classification options were also compared at the time: file the issue directly under "visible tiles", or describe it directly as a defect in "releasing tiles with empty content". The former would conflate invisibility on screen with whether internal objects are still retained; the latter would treat a content state that had not yet been verified as fact. Neither naming option was therefore adopted. The page retains the imprecise old name "Invisible Geometry Tile Lock" so that existing searches and old links still lead to the same place.

## What Can Be Confirmed from the File

The file header for the frozen entry point provides a set of direct connections, not a complete call chain:

```js
import { WebGLArrayRenderTarget, MeshBasicMaterial, DataTexture, REVISION } from 'three';
import { FullScreenQuad } from 'three/addons/postprocessing/Pass.js';
import { ExpandingBatchedMesh } from './ExpandingBatchedMesh.js';
import { convertMapToArrayTexture, isColorWhite } from './utilities.js';
```

This set of imports is enough to indicate that, when opening the file, attention should first be focused on local objects such as batched meshes, textures, and render targets. It provides neither a definition of "Invisible Geometry Tile Lock" nor the conditions that trigger content release. The old page treated `ExpandingBatchedMesh` as direct evidence of the lock, but that claim no longer holds; an import relationship only establishes a direct dependency between files.

`FullScreenQuad` and `WebGLArrayRenderTarget` should not be used to infer the layer at which visibility decisions are made either. They are clues for examining rendering connections, not labels for state ownership. In particular, seeing a texture-conversion helper does not justify collapsing image overlays, MVT annotations, and the lifecycle of geometry tiles into a single path. They may be adjacent at runtime, but this record does not retain enough material to establish that they are handled together.

## Classification Options Considered at the Time

| Option | Benefit at the time | Reason it was not accepted |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Classify the issue as a batching plugin defect | A centralized entry point, low lookup cost | The file path was only the starting point of the earlier investigation, so it cannot establish implementation ownership |
| Treat invisibility directly as a condition for content release | The name seemed close to "lock" | No retained state-change or release records support this equivalence |
| Assign the issue to the download or processing queue | Queues also affect how long resources are retained | No evidence shows that this behavior was triggered by queue capacity or cancellation semantics |
| Retain it as a Quality and Regression item, with a local entry point attached | Preserves the old search path and the boundaries that remain to be investigated | Cannot provide a conclusion in a single pass, and further object-by-object review is still needed |

The fourth option was ultimately adopted. This decision was not "no decision", but an explicit refusal to substitute a vague failure name for a state definition. The page preserves the boundaries that were explicitly kept separate at the time, while code review fills in the relationships later. The related card GEO-206 serves only as navigation; status changes on the card do not automatically become technical conclusions here.

## Samples and Unconfirmed Items

Sample attachments appeared in later materials. The value of a sample is to bring the discussion back from abstract names to inspectable input, but the attachment itself did not establish the lock's responsibility boundaries. When retaining it, the question is not "is there a sample", but whether the sample shows geometry not entering the visible set, content still being retained, or a particular batched object continuing to be processed. These three cases can look similar in the same view, but must not be substituted for one another in the record.

During the same period, the status "one unconfirmed point" was also retained. No specific function, resource type, or recovery outcome has been added to that status here, because the existing materials do not provide those details. The previous version described "not yet confirmed" as "equivalent to an edge case", which should now be treated as an overgeneralization: it is the responsibility relationship that remains unconfirmed, rather than an issue already narrowed down to a particular geometric condition.

## Decision on Responsibility Boundaries

The decision was to retain three levels of responsibility boundaries, rather than assign a single "lock owner".

The first level is the boundary of the observed behavior: Invisible Geometry Tile Lock is the name used for searches in the quality regression materials. It can lead people to the historical issue, but cannot replace distinctions between visibility, content, and processing state.

The second level is the code entry point: `BatchedTilesPlugin.js` is the first place to look left by the earlier investigation. Local connections between batched meshes and rendering resources should be examined here; if the relationship cannot be traced beyond a reference, conclusions cannot be extended on the basis of the filename.

The third level is the state boundary: visible tiles, release of tiles with empty content, shared image-processing queue capacity, and overlay download scheduling may all relate to resource retention, but this record has not determined the causal order among them. Listing these terms together is intended to avoid overlooking neighboring concepts, not to declare that they share a single lock.

This layered approach seemed conservative at the time, at the cost of requiring reviewers to examine states separately rather than directly apply old conclusions. It was still chosen because assigning responsibility prematurely to a particular file, queue, or content branch would later steer regression checks toward the wrong object.

## Addendum for Month 9, 2025

GEO-206 subsequently recorded that a sample had been attached and the status had moved from Pending to In Progress. These two actions show that follow-up continued, but do not document completion of verification. The page previously treated "a sample is available" as a sign that the issue was nearing closure, and that assessment needs correction: a sample expands what can be reviewed, but cannot replace confirmation of the implementation relationships.

This addendum has not copied the actions from the card into the main decision text one by one, nor has it revised the original classification choice on that basis. The reason for retaining the old choice is simple: it concerns how to avoid incorrectly merging objects, not judging the outcome of a particular sample. If later investigation finds that the entry point is not in the batching plugin, the old entry point should still be retained for historical navigation, with the actual relationships listed separately in new materials.

## Verification Entry Points Still Available

After opening `src/three/plugins/batched/BatchedTilesPlugin.js` from the frozen revision, first confirm whether you see the import connections described above or whether the file's contents have already changed. If you still start with the issue name, it can only be used as a search clue; do not map "geometry", "invisible", or "lock" in the name word for word to a single object.

Keep the inspection order as follows: first record geometry tiles and visible tiles separately, then check whether the content is empty, and lastly consider whether batching resources, the download queue, or the processing queue need to be included in the same review. "Lastly" here refers to the order of recording, not runtime sequence. The previous version did not distinguish these two levels, making it easy to mistake investigation steps for the implementation flow.

If review yields only the file header and import list, the conclusion should stop at "there are local batch-rendering connections". If only a sample is available, the conclusion should stop at "the sample covers a state that still needs to be distinguished". It is appropriate to update the lock's actual ownership only when the same material identifies both state changes and object relationships. This page currently contains no such update.

## Retained Earlier Proposals

There was once a proposal to turn this page into a complete resource-release specification and list invisibility, empty content, and cancellation of processing as a single set of conditions. That proposal was not implemented. On the one hand, the current entry point reveals only local rendering dependencies; on the other, the related PriorityQueue Cancellation Semantics has a separate work record under DOC-17, so conclusions from another topic cannot be brought here merely to reorganize the page.

Another proposal was to keep only the card links and stop maintaining the source-file entry point. This proposal was not adopted either. For someone investigating historical issues, GEO-206 shows that the issue was followed up, while `BatchedTilesPlugin.js` preserves the earlier investigation's point of reference; deleting either would prevent later reviewers from distinguishing "where people looked at the time" from "what was proven at the time".

The record therefore retains its incomplete form: the old name, the old entry point, and later unconfirmed items coexist. It can help avoid returning to the same attribution, but should not be treated as the final implementation description for Invisible Geometry Tile Lock.

## Verification State Diagram

The diagram below shows only how the ownership assessment may proceed under this record, not that runtime objects change in the order shown.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> HistoricalName: Retain the old issue name
    HistoricalName --> LocalEntry: Open BatchedTilesPlugin.js
    LocalEntry --> LocalAdjacency: Only local batch-rendering connections confirmed
    LocalAdjacency --> BoundaryPending: State and object relationships have not yet both been confirmed
    BoundaryPending --> BoundaryPending: Only a sample or file header is available
    BoundaryPending --> OwnershipUpdated: The same material provides state changes and object relationships
```

# Queue Cancellation Semantics Proposal

After review, keep both options open. A makes `remove` responsible only for removing items from the waiting queue; any `priority job` already dequeued continues with the existing `promise` result. B passes cancellation to the running `job`, and the caller then distinguishes cancellation from failure. A is a small change, but may leave work running; B has clearer semantics, but would affect `AbortSignal` and callers.

The recommendation at this point is to start with a minimal diff for A, record the queue state before and after `add` and `remove`, and post the result returned by one real call back to GEO-207. If review finds that already-dequeued items are still treated as normal completions, withdraw A and investigate B instead. Still unanswered here: when cancellation happens after dequeueing, who exactly ends `promise`; the owner has not been added either. Removing a pending item rejects the promise from its add with an AbortError, and that rejection is a DOMException.

# Annotation Self-Occupancy Exemption Migration Notes

This page was originally just an entry-point migration draft. It followed the issue name and call name to `test/three/Ellipsoid.test.js`, then treated this file as the verification location for "Annotation Self-Occupancy Exemption". This landing point was never dismantled afterward, so when the page is opened now, the reader sees a test file, several math types, and an unfinished compatibility assessment at the same time.

## Route Left by the Old Page

The old draft actually did very little: it kept a filename, listed the imports in the file header, and put "Annotation Self-Occupancy Exemption" in the compatibility-check heading. It did not record a call chain from the annotation object to `Ellipsoid`, nor did it provide an assertion that could be used to determine whether the exemption holds. The old judgment remains here: since the issue name can point to this test entry point, first treat that entry point as the migrated check location.

This sentence cannot be treated as evidence of current implementation ownership. It was merely the old page's working convention when review was missing. At the time, the page also placed "finding the file" and "finding the behavior" too close together, so people could later jump directly from a path to a conclusion. Do not remove this historical jump, so that this page is not made to look like a migration guide that had clear boundaries from the beginning.

## Entering the Current Check from the Old Path

The relationship between the old path and the current check path is shown below; the arrows indicate page navigation, not implementation calls:

```text
Issue name / call name
      |
      v
internal/tiles-renderer-runtime@v_prev
      |
      |  test/three/Ellipsoid.test.js
      v
Current revision at the same path
      |
      v
Check file-header declarations, test objects, and actual assertions
```

During migration, first retain the original pointer to `v_prev`. Then open `test/three/Ellipsoid.test.js` in the current revision and confirm that the file still begins with the same object relationship. The direct dependencies visible here are:

```js
import * as Cesium from 'cesium';
import { Vector3, MathUtils, Matrix4 } from 'three';
import { Ellipsoid } from '../../src/three/renderer/math/Ellipsoid.js';
import { WGS84_HEIGHT, WGS84_RADIUS } from '../../src/core/renderer/constants.js';
```

These four groups of declarations show the Cesium namespace touched by the test, three's `Vector3`, `MathUtils`, and `Matrix4`, the local import from `Ellipsoid`, and the height and radius constants. They are enough to help someone get from the old entry point back to the current file, but not enough to prove that "Annotation Self-Occupancy Exemption" is implemented by any one of these declarations. The review order must keep the declarations and the test body separate in the record: first confirm the file entry point, then see what the test actually created or compared, and only then decide whether it can still be used as a compatibility-check entry point.

## Actual Actions in the Migration Batch

The first step is to handle the old link. The page originally pointed to `v_prev` in `internal/tiles-renderer-runtime`, and this reference cannot be silently replaced with an unrecorded path. Open the old revision first and confirm that the original filename and the four groups of imports are still on the same navigation trail; if the filename or direct declarations have changed, write the difference in the current paragraph instead of rewriting the old link as a current fact.

The second step is to handle the current file. The current check starts at `test/three/Ellipsoid.test.js`, rather than inferring the implementation from "exemption" in the title. When searching, retain these object names: `Ellipsoid`, `Vector3`, `MathUtils`, `Matrix4`, `WGS84_HEIGHT`, and `WGS84_RADIUS`. The file header shows dependency adjacency; only the uses and assertions in the test body can show what this test actually covers.

The third step is to distinguish compatibility callers. The only caller evidence here is the test file itself. `import * as Cesium from 'cesium';` means that the test imported the Cesium namespace, and `import { Vector3, MathUtils, Matrix4 } from 'three';` means that it imported three names from three; they cannot be expanded into callers that MVT marks as already verified by the runtime. `Ellipsoid` comes from `../../src/three/renderer/math/Ellipsoid.js`, and the constants come from `../../src/core/renderer/constants.js`. These two relative paths can serve as entry points for continued reading, but they are not compatibility results.

Only the fourth step is to update the card navigation. The historical observation for GEO-209 was "the specific usage of Annotation Self-Occupancy Exemption is abnormal". The card's TODO asks the corresponding module maintainer to verify behavior in the current version and identifies an entry point for further checking. After migration, the card still serves only as an entry point: coming in through GEO-209 reaches this page, and from this page one can return to `test/three/Ellipsoid.test.js`. Do not turn the card's abnormality description into a conclusion that the test has already proven; the current page must not describe the card action as a successful verification either.

## Why the Old Wording Remains Visible

This is not a clean new path. The old page treated "the issue name can point to a test file" as sufficient migration evidence. Later review only added the entry point and the unconfirmed portions; it did not comprehensively turn the old wording into a new conclusion. As a result, this page retains three easily confused things: the link to the old revision, the file entry point in the current revision, and the position of "Annotation Self-Occupancy Exemption", for which no local assertion has yet been found on this page.

If all that is needed is to restore the historical investigation, it can stop at `v_prev` and the file header. That gives the route originally used, not a description of current behavior. If compatibility checking is to continue, it must start from the current file body and record the objects used by the test and the comparison results. The mere presence of `Ellipsoid`, `WGS84_HEIGHT`, and `WGS84_RADIUS` in the file header cannot expand the exemption scope to all annotations, all tiles, or all rendering paths; this page has no such material.

The old page's convenient wording that "the same path means the same entry point" is also retained, but current operations should downgrade it to a navigation rule. The current revision may retain a same-named file, or it may retain only partial adjacency; in either case, the page should first display the declarations actually observed and then leave the differences for the reviewer to assess. No new implementation filename is supplied here because the frozen material only provided `test/three/Ellipsoid.test.js`.

## Where to Return on Failure

If the file in the current revision can no longer support the original lookup sequence, rollback restores only the documentation entry, not the source code. Restore the page pointer to `v_prev` under `internal/tiles-renderer-runtime`, retain the file-header differences found in the current revision, and keep the original entry linked at GEO-209. This makes it possible to retrace the old investigation route without misreporting the old path as current behavior.

If the current file still exists but the test body contains no local use corresponding to "Annotation Self-Occupancy Exemption", do not fill the gap from the title. Leave the status as "Entry found, behavior not determined." The next check still starts from that file: first inspect the actual use of `Ellipsoid`, then check whether `Vector3`, `MathUtils`, and `Matrix4` are merely test fixture data, and finally confirm whether the two WGS84 constants participate in the comparison. Without corresponding body material, import names cannot be written as verification results.

## Boundary with Adjacent Records

DOC-20 records another work artifact concerning "Polyline Screen Projection Cache". It cannot be used to fill in the call relationship for "Annotation Self-Occupancy Exemption" on this page. Both pages belong to the same runtime, but their entry objects differ; this page migrates only along GEO-209 and `test/three/Ellipsoid.test.js`. When the other artifact is needed, enter it through the relevant document entry rather than joining the two behaviors here.

This page is also not responsible for providing the complete compatibility matrix for MVT-R2026.09. It preserves how an old investigation location is migrated to the current file, and why this migration still cannot by itself settle the behavior determination. The old link, the four groups of imports, the anomaly description for GEO-209, and the current unconfirmed items must all remain; if any one of them is deleted, readers can no longer distinguish the original entry, the current check location, and the still-unanswered exemption question.

# Polyline Projection Cache Trial Run Notes

The first draft kept the question narrow: after a polyline has been projected onto the screen, does the next check still recompute it point by point? At the time, there was only one starting point for reading the code: `src/three/renderer/controls/EnvironmentControls.js`. There was no polyline sample, no call stack, and no output for comparing two checks.

The first draft's statement that "the cache may be on the controls side" is retained here. At the time, it was only a judgment about where the cache belonged based on the filename. No supporting evidence turned up later, so it can no longer be treated as the implementation location. That earlier judgment did not explain whether the cache key was based on the polyline itself or the projection context; behavior for empty input and duplicate points was never recorded either.

## What the Follow-up Review Left Behind

The later review still started from `EnvironmentControls.js`, but did not identify the object holding the cache. This is a useful place to look for local relationships involving polylines, screen, and projection, then decide from the actual call sites whether to keep tracing. - Input: one polyline; the point count, coordinates, and whether it contained duplicate points were not recorded.
- Operation: trigger projection repeatedly under the same screen conditions.
- Observation: whether projection is recomputed for each point during the second check, and whether a single context change invalidates the result.

# Duplicate-Point Annotation LoD Decision Record

The decision ultimately retained in this record is narrow: `example/r3f/components/makeRotateAroundPoint.js` is a navigation point left over from an earlier investigation, not the confirmed implementation owner for duplicate-point annotation LoD. Relationships must be assessed by referring back to the `v_prev` reference material for `internal/tiles-renderer-runtime`; the file header currently supports only one direct dependency:

```js
import { Matrix4 } from 'three';
```

This decision did not change the requirement name, nor did it fill in a nonexistent call graph for any module. It records a reasoning process that started with matched terms and later separated search leads from functional ownership.

## How the entry point was retained

The initial page had no runtime logs or screenshots of annotation results. Only three pieces of evidence could be recovered: the requirement object "Duplicate-Point Annotation LoD Refinement", the path `example/r3f/components/makeRotateAroundPoint.js`, and the two matching terms `point` and `one` derived from the issue name and call name.

This made the path seem reasonable at first. `makeRotateAroundPoint.js` both has naming suggestive of `Point` and is mentioned in the earlier investigation notes; for someone looking for the next file to inspect, it is indeed more useful than a completely unrelated path. But a "useful search landing point" and "where the requirement is actually implemented" are not the same assessment. The earlier notes did not also provide callers, returned objects, runtime branches, or annotation data, so the page cannot infer those relationships from the matched terms.

The working hypothesis retained in the early draft was: this file might be related to duplicate-point processing. This hypothesis was not presented as a confirmed fact. It explains why the file entered the investigation, but it cannot explain how duplicate points are merged, how LoD is selected, or how display conditions are calculated, nor can it explain whether this file touches MVT annotations. Although those objects appear in the requirement name, the currently retained source code snippet does not connect them to this file.

## Two Routes for Tracing Back

The route of tracing back by name is straightforward. First, use "Duplicate-Point Annotation LoD Refinement" as the issue name, then search paths using `point` and `one`, and finally interpret the matched file as a local implementation. The advantage of this route is that it does not miss the candidate entry point at hand; its disadvantage is that it collapses word similarity, file naming, and code references into the same level of evidence. Unless subsequent readers check again, they may treat a search result as an ownership boundary.

Tracing back through revision references is the slower route. The path is still retained, but only as a key to accessing the material; next, we need to confirm who references this file in `v_prev` and whether those references connect to the requirement object on this page. The only in-file declaration currently frozen is the import of `Matrix4`, so the adjacent relationships this page can explicitly document go no further than that. Without actual reference snippets, we cannot infer the caller of the rotation operation from `Matrix4`, nor can we infer its position in the annotation pipeline from the filename.

The two routes are not mutually exclusive. The name-based route is suitable for finding candidate files, while the revision route is suitable for confirming object relationships. The problem lies in treating the results of the first route directly as the conclusions of the second. The current decision is precisely to separate these two steps: retain the hit first, then wait for reference verification.

At the time, what could actually be compared was not a complete algorithm, but how this record should handle an entry point with insufficient evidence.

# Default MVT Annotation Driver Proposal

We now need to settle one choice for label integration: when no label driver is explicitly provided, should the renderer automatically use the MVT label driver? This is about the default, not reordering tile traversal or replacing existing custom labeling entry points.

The initial preference is to honor the caller's explicit choice. If the caller passes a driver, that choice should still be honored; only when none is passed should it fall back to the MVT default. This lets existing integrations keep their own labeling approach and lets paths that only need MVT labeling skip one layer of initialization.

Start the investigation in `src/core/renderer/tiles/TilesRendererBase.js`. The file contains `LRUCache`, `PriorityQueue`, and `runTraversal`, so setting the default should not also change how caching, queues, or traversal are handled. The driver creation point, along with who owns and releases it after creation, needs to be confirmed separately.

The "all callers must pass a driver" approach is not being adopted at this stage; it turns default behavior into an integration burden. An approach where the default overrides an explicit choice is also not being adopted. Follow-up checks need to use one entry point with no driver supplied and one with an explicit driver to verify whether the two paths remain distinguishable.

# Default MVT Annotation Driver Proposal

The first draft framed this issue as an entry-point default. The direction is unchanged, but the selection boundary needs to be made explicit. The MVT-marked annotation driver is not a new scheduling layer intended to take over tile traversal, downloading, or caching; it only fills the gap where the caller does not provide an annotation driver. Explicit selection remains part of the API and must not lose precedence because a default is added.

This review starts with `src/core/renderer/tiles/TilesRendererBase.js`. The objects directly adjacent to the file header are:

```js
import { getUrlExtension } from '../utilities/urlExtension.js';
import { LRUCache } from '../utilities/LRUCache.js';
import { PriorityQueue } from '../utilities/PriorityQueue.js';
import { runTraversal } from './traverseFunctions.js';
```

These imports indicate that changes to the default driver must stay clear of the existing cache, priority queue, and traversal adjacency objects; they do not themselves indicate which object should own the annotation driver. The proposal must not infer ownership from the filename or split up these existing responsibilities just to add a default.

There were three options on the table.

- Require every caller to provide a driver. The interface is the most direct, but callers that use only the MVT annotation still have to construct an object that the runtime could otherwise provide.
- Always use the MVT-marked driver and ignore the caller's choice. This removes a branch from the entry point, but turns existing custom integrations into ineffective arguments.
- When the caller provides a choice, retain its driver; when no choice is provided, use the MVT-marked driver. This centralizes the default behavior at one entry point while still allowing the caller to bypass it explicitly.

This round proposes the third option. The API semantics can be stated in two sentences: when the caller passes an annotation driver, the renderer uses it; when the caller does not pass one, the renderer uses the MVT-marked annotation driver. Here, "not passed" means that no choice was provided during creation; it does not imply that this proposal supports temporarily replacing the driver at runtime. If runtime switching is genuinely needed later, it should be discussed through a separate interface rather than folded into the default branch.

The default's responsibility also needs to be narrower. It provides a usable path marked MVT; it does not guess which custom annotation the caller originally wanted or repair the lifecycle of a custom driver on the caller's behalf. Explicit and default drivers should converge at the same selection point, so the downstream rendering flow sees only the driver already selected. This avoids checking the default condition again during traversal and does not make `PriorityQueue` or `LRUCache` responsible for annotation policy.

Integration migration should be handled separately by invocation pattern. Existing callers with an explicit driver do not need to remove their configuration or rewrite it as MVT. Callers that only want to use the default MVT-marked annotation Fang Ke can stop creating an equivalent driver object, but should first confirm that their entry point does not depend on behavior bundled with the custom driver. New callers should use the default path only when they have no additional annotation strategy; when customization is needed, they should still provide a driver explicitly. This is therefore not a one-time full replacement; it allows both choices to coexist.

To determine whether the proposal is viable, check at least two things. First, an entry point that provides no driver can reach the path marked MVT; second, an entry point that provides a custom driver is not overridden by the default. The focus of the check is the selection result, not accidental consistency in visual details: the fact that both paths render does not prove that one was not silently replaced by the other. When comparing with existing examples or tests, keep the default and explicit entry points separate to avoid covering only one of them.

Rollback conditions are also limited to the API boundary. If the default prevents an explicit driver from preserving its original selection, roll back and restore an entry point that requires the caller to provide a driver explicitly. If implementing the default requires changing the responsibilities of tile traversal, caching, or the queue, stop treating it as a small interface adjustment. If the MVT default driver cannot be created reliably without additional global configuration, do not fill the gap with implicit configuration; at that point, re-evaluate the two paths: "caller provides a driver" and "add an explicit configuration option."

Three items remain open: where driver selection is carried in the existing creation parameters; whether the default driver's destruction boundary is the same as the explicit driver's; and whether the no-driver user path already has reusable coverage. GEO-212 is used to record coverage and gaps for this default path. The depth-channel discussion is not decided here; related runtime investigation remains in DOC-23.

This proposal only claims that default and explicit selection can coexist. The creation point and lifecycle still need to be confirmed before implementation against the existing interface.

# DRAW_THROUGH Depth Troubleshooting Tree

This page preserves an old troubleshooting path. It is still cited because issues with `DRAW_THROUGH` often first surface as a screenshot, which only shows that the front-to-back ordering is not as expected, without showing which entry point the caller selected or whether both depth-related paths were involved at the same time. Older records grouped these reports under "dual-channel anomalies"; that label is useful for finding people and files, not for attributing a cause.

First, state the symptom in a sentence that can be checked again. For example: which visual element was seen in the wrong front-to-back position, what relationship the caller expected, and which version the screenshot came from. Do not merge "appears to show through" and "appears not to show through" into the same symptom. The former may mean something remains visible when occlusion is expected, while the latter may mean something is occluded when it is expected to be in front; without the entry point and raw output, both statements are still just descriptions from the field.

```text
Received a regression related to DRAW_THROUGH
│
├─ Only a screenshot?
│  ├─ Yes: preserve the visual conditions shown in the screenshot; request the original failure, version, and call entry point
│  └─ No: save the raw output alongside the visual conditions
│
├─ Can the call entry point be located?
│  ├─ No: do not infer the implementation from the name; stop here
│  └─ Yes: confirm the version used by the entry point, then trace back to TilesRendererBase.js
│
├─ Can the rendering / mode selection be determined from the same entry point?
│  ├─ No: record this as missing caller-side information, and do not make a pass comparison
│  └─ Yes: continue by confirming which pass corresponds to the observed depth relationship
│
└─ Do the two sets of material come from the same version and the same entry point?
   ├─ No: split them into two records; they cannot corroborate each other
   └─ Yes: compare the differences, and record only the states already observed
```

"Stopping" here matters. The old page was once treated as a troubleshooting checklist that could provide a conclusion directly, but it actually covers only the narrow stretch from a visual report back to the rendering entry point. If the caller cannot identify the entry point, or the attachments do not include the original failure, continuing to dig through modules will only make guesses look more like conclusions. Recording what needs to be requested is more useful than choosing a seemingly plausible pass.

## First, Distinguish Three Ways of Describing the View

On call, it is especially easy to conflate a few similar terms. The record can be brief, but it must at least distinguish:

- **Occlusion relationship**: one object is in front of or behind another. This is a visual observation, and does not mean the depth path in use is already known.
- **Overlay relationship**: the front-to-back order of the image overlay and the tile view. It has its own adjacent download and processing code, and should not be grouped with annotation issues simply because both appear on screen.
- **Annotation relationship**: the visibility of the MVT annotation in the view. It may also appear in the same frame as geometry tiles, but a screenshot alone cannot establish that it shares a cause with the overlay.

If a report only says "the depth is wrong," first ask the caller to choose one of these descriptions, or retain the original wording and mark it as unclassified. This is not about making the record look tidy, but about preventing someone later from using overlay behavior to explain annotations, or conversely substituting the occlusion of annotations in the view for observations of geometry tiles.

## The Old Path for Tracing Back to the Entry Point

Older records used `src/core/renderer/tiles/TilesRendererBase.js` as the first code entry point. The following adjacent references are visible at the top of that file:

```js
import { getUrlExtension } from '../utilities/urlExtension.js';
import { LRUCache } from '../utilities/LRUCache.js';
import { PriorityQueue } from '../utilities/PriorityQueue.js';
import { runTraversal } from './traverseFunctions.js';
```

These imports have limited but specific value for troubleshooting: they show that references to URL type checks, caching, priority queues, and traversal can all be found near this file. If the field report also involves download queueing, content release, or traversal changes, list them separately as concurrent observations; do not present them as evidence that the depth pass has failed. Conversely, if the visual report already identifies a rendering call, record only its selected `rendering`, `mode`, and whether `depth` or `pass` can be located. These terms were used as navigational cues in the old trace-back process, not as a list of fields or fixed call parameters.

The source version used by the entry point must also be recorded separately. The old troubleshooting path points to an earlier module record; directly comparing "whether a mode with the same name still renders this way" across different versions will misreport a version difference as a regression. If the version cannot be obtained, record "version not provided," and do not infer a version from the screenshot.

## The Two Branches Originally Retained

The initial draft had simple branches: first check whether the depth pass was "enabled," then whether the view returned to normal. That method later proved insufficient, but it is still retained here because some old links point only to this page.

**Old Branch A: The call entry point is visible.** The approach at the time was to follow the entry point back to `TilesRendererBase.js`, look for decision points related to rendering, mode, depth, and pass, then write the observed state in the regression record. This branch can still narrow the scope of code reading; by itself, it cannot prove that a particular decision point caused the visual anomaly. The link between a caller-side state and a screenshot still lacks the original failure and a same-version reproduction.

**Old Branch B: The call entry point is not visible.** The initial draft sometimes suggested first comparing different visual conditions. This is now an outdated shortcut: visual conditions are not the same as call conditions, especially when screenshots are all that remain. Now stop directly at this branch and request the entry point, version, and raw output. Decide whether to continue only after obtaining any one of these, and do not change "possible" to "confirmed" just to complete the investigation.

**Old Branch C: A queue or cache is suspected of affecting the view.** `PriorityQueue` and `LRUCache` are indeed visible at the top of the file, but this only indicates adjacent code to read. If queue, content, or cache behavior occurs at the same time in the field, record it as a parallel lead; unless the original material connects it to the depth relationship, do not combine the two into a single recovery action on this page.

## Gaps Left by This Review

The goal of the related task GEO-213 was to find a caller still using this name and verify the actual version, entry point, and current result. The task was in progress and was later blocked; the recorded reason was that the attachments contained only screenshots, and the original failure had not been obtained. This status explains why no new conclusions of "reproduced" or "recovered" have been added to this page.

The screenshot is still worth preserving because it can pin down the visual relationship reported at the time; it cannot answer the following questions: exactly where the call entry point is, which version the screenshot corresponds to, whether the view can be reproduced consistently, and whether the observed differences come from the same depth pass. If the original failure is obtained later, first place it alongside the screenshot, and do not overwrite or replace the old attachments. If the two sets of material are inconsistent, preserve the inconsistency itself and state in the record which set is missing the entry point or version.

## Actions After Obtaining the Material

Once you have the call entry point, proceed in the following order, without reading all the adjacent code in one go.

1. First confirm whether the entry point is still from the version in the report. If the version differs, add a separate line to the record, and do not use the old screenshot as a direct comparison.
2. Record the rendering or mode selection visible on the caller side. If only a name is visible, preserve the name as is without inferring its meaning.
3. Return to `TilesRendererBase.js`, and continue only through code adjacent to that selection. If your reading leads to `runTraversal`, queues, caches, or URL checks, first state what kind of concurrent lead this is, then decide whether it is related to the view.
4. Once you have an identifiable depth or pass observation, compare it with the original failure. If the two do not match, write "entry point and output not aligned," and do not choose one of them as the answer.

Sometimes the caller will want an immediate recovery recommendation. This page does not provide a recovery switch that can be used independently of the entry point. Interim handling should be limited to preserving the current material, avoiding overwriting attachments, and waiting for an entry point that can be located; any action that changes the rendering mode or depth path must be verified by the actual caller side before it is taken.

## Record Format

When adding material, you can append it using the short format below, leaving empty fields empty without filling them with guesses:

```text
Visual relationship:
Call entry point:
Version:
Original failure:
Visible rendering / mode:
Locatable depth / pass:
Concurrent leads (queues, cache, traversal, or URL):
Whether the screenshot and original failure use the same entry point:
Where this investigation stopped:
```

This format deliberately omits a "root cause" field. For old records of this kind, it is more reliable to first state clearly where the investigation stopped: if the original failure is missing, stop at the attachments; if the entry point is missing, stop at the caller; if the versions differ, stop at version comparison. Once the material can connect the view, entry point, and version, add conclusions in the actual review record.

# Quality Signal Console Handoff Troubleshooting Tree

Treat "stuck" first as an entry-side symptom: at the end of the window, the current result has still not been updated, and occupancy by the old task continues. This symptom is not enough to establish whether the cause is the signal itself, the entry point's state, or permissions; it only means that the evidence from that moment must not be overwritten by later green results. The first step is not to rerun, nor to infer intermediate states from the final display, but to find the first record for the current entry point after the change.

The retained materials are stored in `docs/adj-core/runbooks/core-quality-signal-who-to-escalate-to-when-stuck.md`. This path is an entry point maintained by core · Quality Signal Board. Follow the tree only as far as new records can be provided; if a branch has no records, stop that branch. Recovery on another branch later cannot supply a cause for this branch, nor can consolidated output replace the earliest retained failure sample.

## Preserve the original state first

Before starting, document the current entry point and identify the current revision after the change. Then find the first result recorded for this entry point after the change. Here, "first" does not mean a representative sample selected from multiple runs, or a record that looks more complete in hindsight; it means the material that appeared first at the time and may later have been covered up by green results.

Even if only a screenshot, an old link, or incomplete output remains of the first record, retain it. You may describe what is visible and what is missing, but must not fill in fields from memory, much less move fields from a later run into the first record. Keep the entry point, current revision, and first visible result side by side. All subsequent comparisons, rollbacks, or handoffs start from these three items.

```text
Is the first record for the current entry point still present?
├─ No
│  ├─ Record the current entry point and the current revision after the change
│  ├─ Mark "First result missing"
│  ├─ If only an old link or screenshot remains, attach it after the missing-record note
│  └─ Stop: do not discuss root causes or replace it with a later green result
└─ Yes
   ├─ Did occupancy by the old task continue through the end of the window?
   │  ├─ Yes: retain the time at which the result was still not updated and the occupancy state; check the entry-side handoff records first
   │  └─ No: continue comparing the first record with the most recent normal sample
   └─ Can the first difference remain within the scope of core-quality-signal?
      ├─ Yes: project maintainers continue checking
      └─ No: identify the interface being crossed; if the evidence points to permissions, hand it off to the permissions owner
```

"Stop" in the tree does not mean marking the issue as resolved. It means this page no longer has enough material to support the next judgment. When the first record is missing, the only things that can be confirmed are the missing record and the entry point's location; do not infer why the task was still there from the state at the end of the window, or treat the start of later handling as evidence that the earlier round had recovered.

## Comparing when the first record is available

When comparing with the most recent normal sample, look only for the first difference whose location can be identified. Do not start by calculating average behavior, or infer intermediate behavior from directory names or the final display. Environmental differences may be noted alongside the records because they may explain why two runs differed; however, they cannot replace the first record or justify combining multiple changes into a single cause.

Change only one condition per comparison. If the entry point and environment both change, even a different result cannot establish which one caused the difference. In that case, stop at "Conditions changed simultaneously" and retain the descriptions of both conditions as they were; if further investigation is needed, find another record in which only one condition changes. The purpose is not to make every troubleshooting round longer, but to prevent the person taking over from treating inseparable differences as proof that an interface boundary has been crossed.

The older materials included `screen occupancy`, `glyph material`, and `show transition`. These terms only mark how far the checks reached at the time. Seeing the first two means the records were reviewed along the corresponding branches; the absence of `show transition` means that round did not have enough material to continue. They are not failure categories, nor are they interchangeable results. A term appearing in records consolidated later does not mean the first record was originally complete.

If the first difference can still remain within core-quality-signal, continue checking within the project. At this point, include the first-record materials and the first difference found in the comparison, rather than handing off only the word "stuck". If explaining the first difference already requires crossing a specific interface, first document which interface is being crossed. Without this step, do not send the issue directly to the shared side or the permissions side.

Once the evidence points to permissions, the tree ends here. When handing it off, include the current entry point, the current revision after the change, the first record, the comparison's stopping point, and the confirmed permissions issue. Do not move all non-permissions checks that still belong within the project out of it just because of one handoff; what is being handed off is the specific matter confirmed to cross the boundary, not the entire situation.

## Do not use retries to wipe the original state

Early records treated retries as a faster way to recover. The problem left by that approach was that green results after retries could easily displace the original failure evidence. The person handling the handoff would see only "already fixed", without knowing what had happened at the earliest entry point. This earlier judgment is retained to explain why the first record is now sought first, not to prohibit retries altogether.

The current approach first preserves the original input, current revision, first visible result, and environmental differences. If these materials are incomplete, a retry may still be a subsequent action, but it must not be documented as recovery of the original state. A green result after a retry only shows that the particular run behaved differently; it cannot retroactively prove that the first record had no problem, or supply a time for the current result that was still not updated at the end of the window.

If a retry is needed, first note beside the original record that the retry occurred after the first record. Keep the retry result and the first result side by side; do not overwrite the former. This lets later readers still distinguish whether the green result appeared at the same entry point or came from a rerun; whether occupancy by the old task persisted or was only recorded at the end of the initial window. Continue marking anything the materials cannot answer as a gap.

## Complete the handoff fields first

A handoff is not passing the word "stuck" to the next maintainer. At a minimum, clearly document where the issue is being handed off from, who is handing it off, who is taking over, and what the original entry point was; also document the node where the tree stopped. GEOB-009 preserved a case of omissions in the first handoff: the original entry point, the person handing off, and the person taking over were not all recorded together. In similar cases, fill in these three items first, then decide whether to continue along the tree.

When the first record is missing, the person taking over should receive the fact "First result missing", not a guessed update time. When occupancy by the old task continues through the end of the window, preserve the occupancy state with the handoff as well. If the current result has not been updated, record only that it has not been updated; do not infer from subsequent actions whether it was ever updated during the window.

If the handoff records can confirm only the entry point, but not the scope of the temporary takeover, fill in that gap first rather than directly assigning a particular permissions owner. DOC-33 retain older materials on the scope of the temporary takeover by adj-core; refer to them here when "who is taking over" cannot be filled in with confirmed information. The two pages serve different purposes: this page preserves the path from the symptom to the stopping point, while DOC-33 preserve the mapping between objects and takeover entry points.

## Record only the first stopping point during rollback

Rollback for the current entry point has not yet been rehearsed. Therefore, when occupancy by the old task continues through the end of the window, do not assume that rollback will necessarily release it, or document a completed risk check as a successful rollback. Before starting the rollback, verify that this round still uses the same current entry point; if the entry point has changed, record the change first, then decide whether comparison is still possible.

Run through one rollback under the conditions at the time, recording only the first stopping point. That point may be at the entry point, a missing first record, occupancy by the old task, or the handoff boundary. Stop when you reach it; do not fill in steps that were never reached as completed. GEOB-011 provide navigation for this type of entry point: occupancy by the old task continued at the end of the window, and no guessed update time was filled in for the current result; the start of subsequent handling does not change that record of the state at the time.

Materials from after rollback must not overwrite the first record from before rollback. Keep the two records side by side: one describes the first symptom after the change, and the other describes where the rollback path actually stopped. This way, the next time someone sees a green result, they can still distinguish whether it represents recovery at the original entry point, an incidental result after a rerun, or a run that never reached the same branch at all.

## Test branches with the opposite condition

One stuck sample is not enough to determine whether the tree's branches are useful. After holding core-quality-signal and the current entry point fixed, add a record under the opposite condition. Exactly what that opposite condition is must come from the situation at the time; no environment, input, or result is assumed here. Its purpose is to test whether the previously selected branch can be overturned, not to write another explanation for an existing conclusion.

When adding a counterexample, still follow the first-record rule: first retain its current revision and first result, then explain which one condition changed compared with the original sample. If no counterexample can be found, retain "Counterexample missing"; do not turn a single sample into an established causal attribution. GEOB-016 provide a navigation entry point for this supplementary record.

GEOB-009 later added a counterexample, but that counterexample does not retroactively prove that the first handoff was complete. Keep handoff gaps and counterexample gaps separate: the former determine whether the next maintainer can take over the situation, while the latter help determine whether the existing branch holds up. Mixing the two makes it easy for a new sample to hide a handoff point that was not clearly documented originally.

## Stop and hand off

Do not extend the investigation on this page in the following cases:

- The current entry point has no first record;
- Multiple conditions change simultaneously in the comparison;
- The first difference cannot remain within the scope of core-quality-signal;
- It is already clear that permissions are what need to be addressed;
- Rollback has reached only the first stopping point;
- The opposite condition is needed but has not yet been provided by the situation at hand.

When the first record is missing or conditions cannot be separated, retain the entry point, current revision, and the gap. When a difference extends beyond the project's scope, identify the interface location before handing it off. Send permissions issues to the permissions owner, along with the confirmed materials. When rollback stops, retain both the pre-rollback and post-rollback records. When a counterexample is missing, continue preserving that gap rather than documenting the existing sample as a final causal attribution.

GEOB-002 are for reviewing the first result for the current entry point after the change; GEOB-011 are for reviewing the stopping point of the unrehearsed rollback; GEOB-009 and GEOB-016 preserve the handoff gap and counterexample gap, respectively. The cards are for navigation only. The person taking over should continue from the confirmed node in the tree, rather than reconstructing an unrecorded situation from later green results, the old task's state, or consolidated descriptions.

# Quality Signal Desk: Temporary Handoff Boundaries

During temporary on-call coverage, the main source of confusion isn't who first sees a failure sample, but who can provide an explanation on behalf of the original maintainer. The split here is clear: the temporary maintainer picks up actions that are due, while the original owner continues to explain the behavior of core-quality-signal. Don't fill in guesses in cells where no original owner is named; leaving them blank is better than giving the on-call person authority to explain the behavior.

The temporary holding location is `docs/adj-core/ownership/adj-core-temporary-takeover-boundary.md`. The earlier Q&A for the three consumer questions is kept separately at DOC-30; this table only addresses whether a temporary handoff is valid. It does not reuse those answers to assign responsibility.

## Handoff Table

| Item received | Who to contact first | What the temporary maintainer can do |
|---|---|---|
| Handling exit actions when they come due | Temporary maintainer | Record the actions that are due and confirm whether someone has picked them up; do not rewrite what the actions mean. |
| Explaining the behavior of core-quality-signal | Original owner | Route the question back to the original owner only; do not make judgments about failure samples or regression attribution on their behalf. |
| Items with no owner named yet | Leave blank | Keep the blank slot and the question; do not assign someone based on adjacent modules or familiarity. |
| Instability signals reported by consumers | Reporter and original owner | The temporary maintainer may attach the item's name to the record, but cannot declare ownership on that basis. |

Here, "the temporary maintainer only handles exit actions when they come due" was the boundary at the time. It did not mean handing core-quality-signal over to the on-call maintainer. The latter still follows the original owner's explanation, even if it is reported in the same place. The reason is simple: due-date handling can be delegated, but explanations of behavior affect later failure samples and regression tiering. The temporary intake cannot take that on based on impressions.

## Old Fields Retained Beside the Intake

The table below preserves the follow-up directions originally left beside the intake. It was never organized into a complete owner table and remains here so that these terms are not later mistaken for confirmed module boundaries.

| Old field | Routing noted at the time | Status on record |
|---|---|---|
| `point LoD` | Module on-call | No specific maintainer name was added. |
| `driver version` | Unconfirmed | Blank slot retained. |
| `character metrics` | Caller to add the name | Not for the temporary maintainer to explain. |
| `screen occupancy` | Noted alongside the context | Not established as an item for handoff. |
| `process queue` | For the record only | Ownership not verified. |

These fields are sometimes treated as a list that can be used directly for reassignment. They are not. An acceptance window needs a repeatable starting point, not a one-off result that merely looks cleaner.

Another view was to maintain the old entry point but record all subsequent phenomena in the same acceptance conclusion. This view was also not adopted. The fact that scheduling, visibility, and label layout occur in the same observation round does not mean they are the same judgment. The first divergence at one layer can only show that the comparison is no longer proceeding along the original common trajectory; it cannot explain the other two layers.

Therefore, the observation order in the window was set as three steps, and the order itself cannot be changed: inspect scheduling first, then visibility, and finally label layout. Here, "first" is not a priority ranking, but a way to preserve the first discernible behavioral divergence. If scheduling diverges first, the later visibility and layout observations no longer serve as evidence for the same acceptance round; if visibility diverges first, layout changes should not continue to be used to fill in the cause of the preceding layer.

The fixed conditions likewise include only these three items: tileset, camera state, and queue input. They are not an environment configuration checklist, much less a requirement to hard-code every runtime condition. The meeting selected them because these three items directly form the common starting point for this round's comparison. Without fixing the same tileset, it is impossible to establish that the observed behavior comes from the same set of tiles; changes in camera state alter the observation vantage for visibility and label layout; and changes in queue input make the scheduling results no longer comparable.

The draft was relatively short and could easily be read as "fixing the three items is enough to pass." That reading is inaccurate. Fixed conditions only allow the window to begin; they do not automatically produce a pass conclusion. The scope eligible for approval remains constrained by the existing materials: the portions covered by the materials can be judged, while the portions not covered remain reservations; adjacent normal phenomena must not be used to turn them into confirmation.

After review, the stopping condition was stated more clearly: the first behavioral divergence means stopping the expansion of the judgment. What stops is the scope of the acceptance judgment, not a requirement to stop all runtime activity, nor a claim that phenomena after the divergence have no value. Later phenomena can serve as clues for the next comparison, but they cannot retroactively change the location of the first divergence observed in this round.

This stopping point particularly affects the handling of label layout. If label layout is the first to differ, the record can only state that, on the condition that no discernible divergence appeared in the first two items, the layout no longer matches the baseline. It cannot establish that scheduling was completely stable, much less attribute the layout change to any particular runtime stage. The draft did not elaborate on this layer; the later addendum preserved this gap rather than filling in the cause through speculation.

Likewise, the absence of a divergence in scheduling does not constitute a guarantee for visibility and label layout. The three-step order is used to locate the earliest difference, not to establish a dependency in which a normal preceding item allows the following item to be skipped. Acceptance still requires observation in order; once the first divergence appears, later observations no longer enter the same pass/fail conclusion.

Retaining the old-package entry point is a hard condition of this decision. Its significance is not to claim that the old package is inherently more reliable, but to give rollback a clear landing point. If the old entry point is removed first within the window and a behavioral divergence is discovered afterward, rollback would face both the entry-point change and the window change at the same time, making it impossible to confirm whether it returned to the original comparison starting point or to another unrecorded intermediate state.

The meeting materials require the rollback steps to be independently executable. Here, independent means that rollback cannot depend on another change in the window having succeeded, nor assume that the observation process left behind no conditions that could affect the comparison. Rollback must first return to the retained old-package entry point; completing this action should not require "perform another window adjustment" as a prerequisite. The cost is greater pressure to retain the new and old arrangements simultaneously within the window, but at the time this cost was considered smaller than the risk of being unable to roll back independently.

The draft did not separately explain the "old-package entry point" and the "current tile-lifecycle entry point," and some people later understood the two as a permanent binding relationship. Here is a correction: this decision only requires retaining the old-package entry point during this round's change window and using the current tile-lifecycle entry point as the comparison starting point. It makes no long-term decision about the ownership, naming, or replacement path of future package entry points.

The window-adjustment approach was not completely rejected. What was rejected was directly using the adjusted window to replace the existing entry point when evidence was insufficient, and treating the result as a completed acceptance conclusion. If this approach is proposed again later, it must at least explain that the comparison starting point remains identifiable and that changes caused by the window itself can be separated from changes in scheduling, visibility, or label layout. This condition was not met in this round, so window adjustment was not approved as an entry-point replacement approach.

"Only approve the scope covered by existing evidence" has a concrete meaning here: the materials support sequential observation under the same tileset, camera state, and queue input, and they support closing out the conclusion at the first behavioral divergence; the materials do not support declaring a layer with no observed divergence to be permanently stable, much less adding unobserved combinations to the approval scope. The draft's wording was relatively brief, and the review did not expand this boundary.

This way of closing out the scope also explains why this record retains the opposing views. Opposing views are not substitutes for action items: they correspond to paths that were genuinely compared during the review. The direct-window-adjustment path was retained because it indicates that any future change to the window must re-establish the comparison relationship; the path of merging all phenomena into one conclusion was retained because it reminds readers not to miswrite the same observation round as a single attribution.

From the perspective of executing the window, the minimum readable record should answer four questions: which entry point the comparison starts from, which inputs are fixed, which layers are observed in sequence, and under what condition judgment stops. This decision gives the respective answers as the current tile-lifecycle entry point, the same tileset/camera state/queue input, scheduling—visibility—label layout, and the first behavioral divergence. Explanations beyond these should not masquerade as content that has already been decided.

The review addendum also retains one unconfirmed point: whether the phenomena at later layers after the first divergence merit opening a separate comparison was not decided in this decision. They may be an outward manifestation of the same change, or they may simply be a new observation entry; the existing record does not support choosing between the two. Leaving this point in place better matches the conclusion at the time than filling it with a seemingly complete handling sequence.

DOC-44 records the handoff for a rendering baseline environment on-call rotation change. It can help explain why an executable rollback action needs to be retained during the window handoff, but it does not change this record's decision on the acceptance scope. The rotation arrangement is not folded into the window judgment here, nor are new acceptance conditions added on that basis.

This material continues to be cited mainly because it retains an obsolete but useful comparison constraint: when the entry point has not yet been replaced and the evidence is incomplete, first fix the common starting point, then close out the judgment at the earliest discernible divergence. It is not equivalent to the operating rules for all current MVT acceptances. The later review only filled in the boundaries that the draft had not made clear; it did not recast the parts that were unconfirmed at the time as established facts.

Finally, the original decision remains in force: this round's acceptance window retains the old-package entry point, with the current tile-lifecycle entry point as the comparison starting point; judgment is limited to the scope covered by the existing materials; scheduling, visibility, and label layout are observed in order; the first behavioral divergence stops any expansion of the conclusion; and rollback must be independently executable. All other issues remain reservations rather than default passes.

## In-Window Judgment Flow

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Retain the old-package entry point] --> B[Fix the same tileset, camera state, and queue input]
    B --> C[Observe scheduling]
    C --> D{First behavioral divergence appears?}
    D -- Yes --> H[Stop expanding this round's conclusion]
    D -- No --> E[Observe visibility]
    E --> F{First behavioral divergence appears?}
    F -- Yes --> H
    F -- No --> G[Observe label layout]
    G --> I{First behavioral divergence appears?}
    I -- Yes --> H
    I -- No --> J[Approve only the scope covered by existing evidence]
    H --> K[Roll back to the old-package entry point using independent steps]
```

This flowchart is an index to this round's comparison and stopping point, and does not expand "no divergence observed" into a long-term stability conclusion.

# Shared tileset Sample Entry Point Guide

Search results are the easiest place to get misled when maintaining shared tileset samples: they return tile-lifecycle, type declarations, sample files, and test names at the same time. They all contain similar terms, but the person taking this over needs the actual entry point, not a catalog of all matches.

This review still starts from tile-lifecycle's public repository entry point. `src/core/renderer/tiles/Tileset.d.ts` remains at the starting point because the first search usually passes through it; it provides object clues for tile and tileset, and gives later backtracking a stable place to return to. It does not establish ownership of shared sample maintenance. Treating a declaration file as the maintenance entry point quickly pulls same-named files into the path by mistake.

The main backtracking path is now fixed as follows:

```text
tile-lifecycle public entry point
        |
        | Keep only call sites that connect directly
        v
One confirmed direct caller
        |
        | Continue by checking who that caller passes the object to
        v
First actual consumer of shared tileset sample maintenance
```

The "one" here does not mean information was omitted; it is an intentional scope limit. There may be more than one similarly named object at the entry point, but this review tracks only the one direct caller actually connected to the public entry point. This lets the person taking over confirm where sample maintenance starts within a call relationship that can be rechecked, without first explaining the entire tile lifecycle.

In step one, when opening the tile-lifecycle entry point, first record the object names that can be traced back to it, then return to `Tileset.d.ts` and compare them with the declarations. The purpose is not to find every place where tileset appears, but to avoid mistaking an adjacent tile concept for the sample object. Names that match in the declarations can be traced further; names that appear only in comments, imports, or sample text do not count as the next hop yet.

The second step accepts direct calls only. A call site must satisfy both conditions: it receives a value or control flow from the entry object, and it can be traced onward to a subsequent object. A same-named import, same-named field, or adjacent directory alone is insufficient for this step. Previously, someone started browsing from a same-named sample file and found related tileset terminology, but never got back to tile-lifecycle; keep that path as a waypoint, not as part of the main path.

After reaching the direct caller, the question changes from "who called the entry point?" to "who first actually consumes the shared sample?" There is no need to enumerate every subsequent use site. Finding the first consumer to read, pass, or maintain the shared tileset sample is enough to answer the most common entry question during handoff: the maintenance work is not inferred from the declaration name; it is reached through this call relationship.

In this review, targeted Vitest output serves only as a locating aid. Keeping the output alongside the call site under review lets us check that this trace has not quietly shifted to another same-named path. The fact that the output reaches tile-lifecycle does not automatically prove that the sample file later in the path is the consumer; conversely, a sample name appearing in test material does not automatically add a call edge. Use the output first to narrow the area of attention, then return to the code relationships to confirm the link between the direct caller and the first consumer.

Keep these two types of material separately: the call site explains "why we followed this path," while the targeted Vitest output explains "which segment was seen during the review." Combining them into one conclusion will make later readers think the test output itself established maintenance ownership. It does not serve that purpose.

A practical check order is:

1. From tile-lifecycle's public entry point, list the object terms to trace in this review.
2. At `Tileset.d.ts`, compare against the declarations, excluding objects that are nearby only because their names match.
3. Find the entry point's direct call site; retain only one path that is definitely connected.
4. Follow that caller onward, stopping at the first actual consumer of shared tileset sample maintenance.
5. Place the targeted Vitest output alongside this path for comparison; do not use it to expand the scope.

Step four is the stopping point for this page. If a new maintenance scope, a different sample convention, or an object relationship requiring explanation from another maintainer appears after the first consumer, leave it as a separate question instead of casually writing it as an established fact. This stopping point is more useful than a string of unverified downstream calls: the next person taking over knows how far the main path has been verified and where to continue asking questions.

After the review, the earlier practice of roughly inferring the sample maintenance location from a same-named file is no longer used. Matching terms can only help with locating; the continuous relationship among the public entry point, direct caller, and first actual consumer is what constitutes this backtrace. If any hop in the middle is missing, return to the entry point and search again instead of filling it in with directory proximity or a test name.

DOC-46 records a deviation during the plugin's public-entry change window. Both pages may contain the phrase "public entry point," but that phrase does not provide call evidence here; when checking shared tileset sample maintenance, still follow this page's path back to tile-lifecycle.

The remaining boundary is narrow: deeper sample-maintenance details after the direct caller have not been covered in this review. If it becomes necessary to cross into another maintenance scope, retain the object name and the last confirmed hop.
